#5479. Certinia brings AI into professional services workflows

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky, chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE. “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier, chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to optimize renewals. Everything we’re doing is ultimately affecting the bottom line.”

Certinia’s long-time relationship with Salesforce is a key element in the company’s overall strategy. Certinia is featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce’s AgentExchange and has provided AI-powered sales and delivery for Salesforce’s consulting partner network.

“We have a deep partnership with Salesforce,” said Raju Malhotra, chief product and technology officer of Certinia. “I spend personally a lot of time with the Salesforce executives on business and engineering, and we collaborate. We bring our customer use cases, they tell us about what’s coming up from a capability perspective and we work very well together. They’re led by a founder [chief executive officer] who’s very much in tune with the market, and they want to stay ahead.”

Certinia has sought to stay ahead in its own right by introducing Veda, an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine that functions as the company’s suite of AI specialist agents and intelligent actions. The solution delivers rules-bound, trusted and ROI-focused autonomous workflows, combining Certinia’s years of institutional memory with advanced AI reasoning. Certinia’s goal with Veda is to provide customers with enough flexibility so that agents integrated into existing business workflows can drive immediate and measurable value.

“We’ve infused Veda throughout the experience for users to be more productive,” Malhotra said. “We have package agents, which are Veda agents. We launched Veda with 10 packages. Now we have 24, and we will finish the year with more than 40 package agents. Those agents are very much persona based, and they help our customers.”

Veda is not simply a layer of generic automation; it represents a key shift in how AI is being used in the enterprise. Certinia’s focus on serving the professional services market motivated the company to ground its AI offering in operational reality, where context, coordination and control matter as much as speed, according to Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Certinia’s recent announcement of Veda is more profound than it may appear on the surface,” he said. “Veda is notable not simply because it introduces a new suite of AI agents and intelligent workflow-based actions, but because it offers a glimpse into what the future of enterprise AI is likely to look like: AI that works alongside humans in consequential workflows, helps people make better decisions and earns trust by being grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.”

Since the launch of Veda in April, Certinia has taken several actions to enhance its AI capabilities. In July, the firm acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform purpose-built for the professional services sector.

This acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can now connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review, according to Hebner.

“Certinia provides the deep, structured foundation of professional services, customer success and financial management; Moonnox brings the missing half: capturing the unstructured reality — the emails, chats, and calls — where delivery actually happens,” he explained. “Together, they fuse everything a services business knows with everything their teams do, moving Veda beyond orchestration toward context-aware, AI-native services delivery.”

The context graph can also draw on structured records such as timecard entries and utilization figures. Moonnox helps bring that information into the graph for client-facing teams managing projects, according to Cesafsky.

“That’s been where Moonnox has really showed up for us over the last couple of months,” he said. “It’s those capabilities to help the client-facing services [and] delivery teams run and operate their projects. [Moonnox] is effectively an intake machine for a lot of that structured data to bring that into the context graph as well.”

In September, Certinia unveiled its System of Action for services businesses. The offering significantly expanded the Veda AI suite with new agents and more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135.

Certinia’s System of Action uses a three-tier architecture to bring AI agents into services workflows. The first tier brings together structured records and unstructured project data. The second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia’s experience in services to inform decisions. The third lets agents act within existing workflows.

“We want to accelerate the delivery for our customers,” Malhotra said. “Our customers are solving some specific problems in the professional services world. We don’t want to just give you a project plan. If you choose to execute that project plan with some agents, we’ll give you that. If you want to really think about agentic capabilities to help you in making money, in expanding your time [and] in terms of delivery, we will help you with that.”

For professional services firms, adopting AI agents means deciding which parts of project delivery to delegate to them.

“We view professional services as a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability,” Hebner said. “If Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Certinia Signal interview series. Neither Certinia, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5478. From Peru to Kenya: 12 countries affected by El Niño

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These countries affected by El Niño, from Peru to Kenya, show how one warm Pacific pattern can bring floods, drought, wildfires and crop losses across the tropics and beyond

A band of unusually warm water in the Pacific Ocean can empty reservoirs in South America, feed fires in Southeast Asia and swell rivers in East Africa. That band has a name, El Niño, and it returns every few years.

The name is Spanish for "the boy" or "the Christ child." Peruvian fishermen gave it to a warm current that appeared off their coast around Christmas. Scientists now use it for a broader event: a warming of sea-surface waters across the central and eastern tropical Pacific.

El Niño recurs irregularly, roughly every two to seven years. A typical episode lasts about nine to 12 months. It is the warm phase of a larger climate cycle known as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO. Its cool counterpart is La Niña.

The main way El Niño reaches distant countries is through rainfall. As the warm water shifts east, the zones of rising air and heavy storms shift with it. Some regions turn wetter than usual, with heavy rain and flooding. Others turn drier, with drought, low rivers and higher fire risk. The pattern is not fixed. Two El Niño events can play out differently, and a country that floods in one episode may escape the next.

Those shifts carry economic consequences. Fisheries, farms, hydropower dams, shipping routes and city water systems all depend on rain arriving when expected. When it doesn't, the effects can travel through food prices, electricity supply and trade.

Three strong events are widely cited as reference points: 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16. Several of the countries below also felt the more recent 2023–24 El Niño.

This list covers 12 countries affected by El Niño, grouped by region. It starts with Peru and Ecuador on South America's Pacific coast, then moves through the rest of the Americas, Southeast Asia, Oceania, South Asia and Africa. It is a selection, not a ranking, and not a complete list. Each entry describes what El Niño tends to bring to that country, along with documented episodes. Weather is rarely the only cause of a flood, a drought or a policy decision. Where El Niño played a part, it is treated as one factor among others.

Peru tends to take two hits in a strong El Niño year. Warm water disrupts the anchovy fishery behind its fishmeal industry, and heavy rain floods a northern coast that is usually desert.

Both effects trace back to the ocean off Peru's shore. In normal years, the Humboldt Current and coastal upwelling bring cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface. That water supports plankton, which feeds vast schools of Peruvian anchovy, known locally as anchoveta. The species, Engraulis ringens, supports a single-species fishery that ranks among the world's biggest by catch volume.

When El Niño warms the coastal sea, upwelling weakens and the cold water retreats. Anchovy schools tend to move deeper or farther south in search of cooler conditions. Catches can fall sharply as a result. Seabirds that feed on the anchovy, such as the Peruvian booby and the Guanay cormorant, also go hungry.

The effects reach well beyond Peru. Most of the anchovy catch is processed into fishmeal and fish oil rather than eaten directly. Peru is one of the world's largest producers of fishmeal, which goes into feed for farmed fish, pigs and poultry. A poor season off Peru can tighten feed supplies for fish farms on other continents.

The fishery has a long history with El Niño. The 1972–73 event, combined with heavy fishing pressure, contributed to a collapse of the anchovy stock. Today, Peruvian authorities set fishing seasons and catch limits based on scientific surveys of the stock. In warm years, those surveys can lead to delayed or shortened seasons.

On land, the problem is too much water. Northern regions such as Piura and Tumbes normally receive little rain. Much of Piura sits on the Sechura Desert. During strong El Niño events, warm offshore water fuels downpours that swell dry riverbeds and overwhelm towns built for arid conditions.

The 1997–98 El Niño brought severe rains to northern Peru. Flooding damaged roads, bridges, homes and farmland across the region.

In 2017, a different kind of event struck. It was classified as a coastal El Niño, or Niño Costero. The warming was concentrated near the coasts of Peru and Ecuador rather than across the wider Pacific. It still caused serious flooding across northern Peru. Mudslides, known in Peru as huaicos, swept through communities in the region.

Peru also runs a national monitoring system for these coastal conditions. It issues alerts when warming develops offshore, giving fishing fleets and northern towns advance notice.

Ecuador feels El Niño in two places at once. Strong events tend to bring heavy rain and flooding to its Pacific coast, while warmer seas around the Galápagos Islands cut off the cold-water food supply that much of the islands' wildlife depends on.

The mainland coast is where people bear most of the impact. Provinces such as Esmeraldas, Manabí, Guayas and El Oro sit on a low coastal plain that drains toward the Pacific. In normal years, much of the southern stretch of that coast is relatively dry. During a strong El Niño, warm water offshore feeds intense, repeated downpours. Rivers and drainage systems cannot carry that much water away.

The 1997–98 event remains the reference point for coastal flooding in Ecuador. Months of heavy rain flooded towns, triggered landslides and washed out roads and bridges along the coast. Broken transport links cut off communities. They also slowed the movement of goods to and from Guayaquil, the country's largest city and main port.

Agriculture on the coast is exposed as well. The lowlands grow much of the country's export produce, including bananas. Ecuador ranks among the world's largest banana exporters. Flooded plantations and waterlogged soils reduce harvests in a wet El Niño year. Damaged roads make it harder to move whatever fruit survives to the docks.

About 900 kilometers offshore, the Galápagos face a different problem. The islands' marine life relies on cold, nutrient-rich water. The Humboldt Current carries some of it north. The Equatorial Undercurrent pushes more of it up from the depths along the western islands. When El Niño warms the surface, that upwelling weakens, and the food chain thins out from the bottom up.

Marine iguanas show the effect clearly. They are the only lizards in the world that forage in the sea, grazing on algae along rocky shorelines. In warm-water years, the red and green algae they prefer die back, and many iguanas starve. Their numbers fell sharply during the strong events of 1982–83 and 1997–98.

Galápagos sea lions struggle too. The fish they hunt move deeper or scatter. Mothers must then travel farther to feed. Pups and juveniles are the most vulnerable, and many die when food runs short. Galápagos penguins and flightless cormorants also depend on cold-water prey. Both suffered heavy losses in 1982–83.

Not every species loses out. Heavy rain turns the normally arid islands green, and land plants, insects and seed-eating finches can multiply. That split between hardship at sea and abundance on land has made the Galápagos a long-running field site for studying how El Niño reshapes an ecosystem.

Colombia tends to turn drier during El Niño. That matters for a country that gets most of its electricity from hydropower. Weak rainfall drains the reservoirs that supply both power stations and city taps. In April 2024, low reservoirs pushed Bogotá into water rationing.

The country's geography explains the exposure. The Andes split into three ranges across Colombia, and rivers descending from them feed a network of hydroelectric dams. Much of the Andean region also has two rainy seasons each year. Those wet spells refill the reservoirs before the drier months.

When El Niño weakens that rainfall, storage falls. The electricity grid then leans harder on thermal plants that burn gas and coal. Those plants cost more to run. Dry years tend to push up wholesale power prices.

Colombia has seen how far that pressure can go. A drought linked to El Niño left reservoirs low in 1992, and the government imposed nationwide electricity rationing. Scheduled blackouts ran for months. Clocks were moved forward an hour to save power, a change known as "la hora Gaviria" after then-President César Gaviria.

Bogotá's 2024 shortage hit water supply rather than power. Most of the capital's drinking water comes from the Chingaza system, a set of reservoirs and tunnels in the mountains east of the city. Months of weak rainfall left its storage at low levels.

The city divided its service area into sectors. Each sector took turns going without water for a day at a time. Residents were also asked to cut their consumption.

The dry spell overlapped with the 2023–24 El Niño, which contributed to the shortfall. It was not the sole cause. Bogotá is one of South America's largest cities. With one main system supplying most of its water, low storage at Chingaza affected millions of residents.

Water stress reaches farms as well. Colombia is one of the world's leading coffee producers. Its growers depend on the timing of rain for flowering and bean development. A prolonged dry season can disrupt that cycle and reduce yields.

For Colombia, much of El Niño's impact comes down to storage. Whether the country gets through an event without cuts depends heavily on how full its reservoirs are when the dry conditions arrive.

El Niño tends to split Brazil in two. Much of the north, including the Amazon $AMZN basin, usually turns drier than normal, while the south tends to get more rain.

That divide matters in a country of Brazil's size. A single event can leave river towns in the Amazon short of water. The same event can push farm states in the far south toward waterlogged fields.

The Rio Negro offers a recent example of the northern side. In October 2023, during an El Niño year, the river at Manaus fell to its lowest level on record. Manaus is the capital of Amazonas state and the largest city in the Brazilian Amazon.

The Rio Negro joins the Solimões River near Manaus, and together they form the main stem of the Amazon. Across much of the region, rivers do the work of roads. Boats carry fuel, food, medicine and passengers between communities that have no highway links. When water levels drop, some channels become too shallow for those boats. Riverside settlements can then be cut off from supplies.

The Rio Negro drains a vast catchment, and its level reflects rainfall across that whole area. El Niño was underway in 2023, but it was not the only factor shaping that year's dry season.

Drier conditions in the Amazon also raise fire risk. Most fires in the region are set by people, often to clear land for pasture or crops. A parched forest allows those fires to spread farther than they would in a wet year.

The semi-arid interior of northeastern Brazil, known as the sertão, also tends toward drought in El Niño years. Smallholder farmers and livestock herders there depend on short seasonal rains. A weak rainy season can cut harvests and strain local water supplies.

The pattern reverses in the south. States such as Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná tend to see above-average rainfall during El Niño. These states are major producers of soybeans, corn and rice. Rio Grande do Sul grows the largest share of Brazil's rice.

Extra rain can delay planting and harvests. It also raises the risk of river flooding in low-lying towns and farmland.

Southern Brazil has flooded in El Niño years, but each flood has several drivers. Local storms, terrain, drainage and land use all play a part. El Niño shifts the odds toward a wetter south. It does not decide the outcome of any single storm.

Effects in Brazil's center and southeast vary more from one event to the next. The north–south contrast is the most consistent El Niño signal in the country.

A severe drought in 2023, to which El Niño contributed, led the Panama Canal Authority to cut daily ship crossings and lower draft limits. Shallower drafts meant many vessels had to carry less cargo to make the passage.

The canal's exposure to drought comes from its design. Since it opened in 1914, the waterway has relied on locks that lift ships up to Gatún Lake and lower them again. Gatún Lake is an artificial reservoir created by damming the Chagres River. When it was completed, it was the largest man-made lake in the world.

Every transit draws on that lake. Gravity moves fresh water from the lake into the lock chambers. That water then flows out to the ocean. The original locks use no pumps to send it back. A long run of ships therefore means a steady drain on the reservoir.

The same lake system also supplies drinking water to much of Panama's population, including Panama City. In a dry year, the canal's needs compete directly with household supply.

Panama depends on its rainy season, which usually runs from about May to December, to refill the reservoir. El Niño tends to bring drier conditions to parts of Central America. In 2023, rainfall fell well short, and the lake dropped low enough that the authority rationed passage.

The newer, larger locks opened in 2016 after an expansion project. They include water-saving basins that reuse part of the water from each lockage. Ships using the older locks have no such system.

The restrictions rippled through global shipping. Vessels waited at anchor for slots, and some operators paid extra in auctions for priority crossings. Others sent ships on longer routes, including through the Suez Canal or around the southern tip of South America.

The canal links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It is a key route for cargo moving between the U.S. East and Gulf coasts and Asia. That reach helps explain why a rainfall shortfall in one Central American country registered in freight markets worldwide.

In Indonesia, El Niño tends to bring a longer, harsher dry season. That raises the risk of fire on the country's carbon-rich peatlands. The 2015 El Niño coincided with major fires that sent thick haze across much of Southeast Asia.

Peat is a waterlogged soil built from layers of partly decayed plant matter. Indonesia holds one of the largest areas of tropical peatland in the world. Most of it lies on Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua. In its natural state, peat stays wet and resists burning.

Much of that land has been drained with canals to grow oil palm and pulpwood trees. Drained peat dries out, and in a drought year it ignites easily. Land is often cleared by burning, and those fires can spread into the dry peat nearby.

Peat fires are hard to put out. They can smolder underground for weeks, out of reach of water dropped from aircraft. They also release large amounts of carbon dioxide and dense smoke.

That smoke crosses borders. In 2015, haze from Indonesian fires drifted over Singapore, Malaysia and other neighbors, disrupting flights and daily life. The strong 1997–98 El Niño had produced a similar regional haze crisis.

Earlier haze episodes led governments to respond with laws and agreements. Singapore passed its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014. The law allows penalties against companies that cause haze affecting the city-state. Indonesia's parliament ratified the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution later that year. In early 2016, President Joko Widodo created a Peatland Restoration Agency to rewet and restore damaged peat.

Farms feel the dry spells as well. Rice is Indonesia's staple food, and much of the crop depends on the timing of the rainy season. When the rains arrive late or fall short, planting is delayed and harvests can shrink.

A weaker harvest puts pressure on the national food supply. Bulog, the state logistics agency, manages rice stocks and imports. Those reserves act as a buffer when domestic output falls. In El Niño years, the same dry weather that feeds the fires can also tighten the country's rice supply.

The 2015–16 El Niño left farms across the Philippines short of rain, and prolonged dry spells damaged crops in several regions. Farming in the country depends heavily on seasonal rainfall. A dry El Niño year can mean smaller harvests and lower rural incomes.

The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands in the western Pacific. Much of its rain arrives with the southwest monsoon, known locally as habagat, and with tropical storms. In El Niño years, rainfall across much of the country tends to drop below normal. The effect is not uniform, and some provinces fare worse than others from one event to the next.

The drying effect of the 2015–16 event stretched into the early months of 2016. That period overlapped with the country's usual dry season, when fields already receive little rain.

Rice is the national staple, and most of it comes from small family farms. Many paddies depend on rainfall rather than irrigation canals. When the rains fail, farmers may delay planting, and crops already in the ground can wither before harvest.

Corn is the country's second major grain crop, and Mindanao, the large southern island group, grows a substantial share of it. Much of that corn is rainfed. Parts of Mindanao were among the farming areas hit by drought during the 2015–16 event.

Irrigated land is not fully shielded either. Angat Dam in Bulacan province supplies most of Metro Manila's water. It also feeds irrigation for farmland in Bulacan and Pampanga. When its reservoir runs low, cities and farms compete for the same supply.

For a farming household, a failed crop cuts into both its food supply and its cash income in the same season. Smallholders with little savings have limited room to absorb that loss before the next planting.

Domestic rice production does not fully meet demand, and the Philippines imports rice to cover the gap. Any shortfall in local harvests has to be made up from domestic stocks or imports.

The 2015–16 El Niño brought drought and frost to Papua New Guinea's highlands. Both damaged the food gardens that most families there rely on. The combination hit communities that grow nearly everything they eat and keep little stored surplus.

The highlands form a chain of mountain valleys running through the center of the island of New Guinea. Provinces such as Enga, Hela, Southern Highlands, Western Highlands, Simbu and Eastern Highlands hold a large share of the country's population. Many of these valleys sit far above the coastal lowlands. That altitude gives them a cooler climate than the rest of the tropical country. Most people there live in rural villages rather than towns.

Sweet potato, known locally as kaukau, is the staple crop across much of the region. Families plant it in mounded gardens and harvest it continuously rather than in a single season. That system works when rain is reliable. It leaves households exposed when gardens stop producing for months at a time.

Frost is the less expected threat in a tropical country. Dry spells tend to bring clear night skies, and clear skies let heat escape from the ground after dark. In high-altitude valleys, temperatures can then drop below freezing. Frost burns sweet potato leaves and can kill the plants outright. The resulting losses show up in harvests well after the cold nights have ended.

Drought added a second strain. Streams and springs that supply drinking water ran low in many areas. Gardens planted in dry soil struggled to establish.

The pattern was not new. The 1997–98 El Niño brought a similar run of drought and frost to the highlands. In that event, crop failures led to widespread food shortages across the region.

The effects of the 2015 dry spell also reached beyond village gardens. Low water on the Fly River in Western Province halted barge traffic that year. The Ok Tedi copper and gold mine suspended operations because it could not ship its concentrate downriver. The mine is one of Papua New Guinea's largest export earners.

Eastern and northern Australia tend to receive less rain in winter and spring during El Niño years. That dry tilt raises bushfire danger and strains farms. It has also coincided with mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.

The timing matters for agriculture. Wheat and barley in the eastern grain belt are sown in autumn. These crops depend on winter and spring rain to fill out before harvest. A dry season at that stage can cut yields sharply. Livestock producers face a parallel problem as pasture dries out, and some sell animals they can no longer feed.

Fire risk climbs alongside the dryness. Low rainfall leaves grass, scrub and forest litter parched heading into the warmer months. El Niño years also tend to bring hotter days across southern Australia. That heat dries the fuel further. The result is a longer window in which a single ignition can spread quickly.

El Niño is not the only driver of a bad fire season. The Indian Ocean Dipole, a separate pattern of sea-surface temperature differences across the Indian Ocean, also shapes Australian rainfall. A positive dipole tends to dry the southeast. The 2019–20 Black Summer fires burned during a strong positive dipole rather than an El Niño. When both patterns line up, the drying can compound.

At sea, the effects show up on the Great Barrier Reef, the coral system stretching along the Queensland coast. Mass bleaching hit the reef in 1998 and again in 2016. Both episodes came at the tail end of strong El Niño events. Bleaching happens when water stays too warm for too long and corals expel the algae living in their tissue. Without those algae, corals lose their color and their main food source.

Bleached coral can recover if temperatures fall soon enough. If the heat lasts, many corals die. The 2016 episode hit the reef's northern section hardest.

Long-term ocean warming adds to the pressure. Each El Niño now arrives on top of higher baseline sea temperatures. The reef bleached again in 2017, a year without El Niño conditions. That repeat showed heat stress can bleach the reef without El Niño.

El Niño years tend to bring India a weaker southwest monsoon, the June-to-September rains that water most of the country's crops. A poor monsoon can shrink harvests and push up food prices across the world's most populous country.

The southwest monsoon delivers the bulk of India's annual rainfall. Farmers time the kharif, or summer, planting season around its arrival. Rice, pulses, soybeans and cotton are among the crops sown as the rains begin. Much of India's cropland has no irrigation and relies on rainfall alone. A late or patchy monsoon therefore reaches farm incomes quickly.

The link is a tendency, not a rule. Several of India's notable drought years, including 2002 and 2009, coincided with El Niño. The strong 1997–98 event, by contrast, passed with a roughly normal monsoon. Conditions in the Indian Ocean matter too. A pattern called the Indian Ocean Dipole can offset or reinforce the Pacific signal. A positive phase of the dipole helped support the rains in 1997.

That uncertainty shapes economic planning. India's weather agency issues a monsoon forecast each spring, and farmers and traders watch it closely. Food makes up a large share of the country's consumer price basket. A weak monsoon can feed directly into inflation.

Rice sits at the center of these concerns. India is the world's largest rice exporter. At home, a public distribution system supplies subsidized grain to hundreds of millions of people. Any threat to the harvest touches both domestic food security and global trade.

In July 2023, India's government banned exports of non-basmati white rice. The move came amid concerns about domestic supply and rising prices. It arrived as an El Niño was developing in the Pacific. NOAA had declared El Niño conditions in June 2023. Basmati rice was not covered by the ban.

The decision's effects reached well beyond India. Many importing countries in Asia and Africa depend on Indian rice. Buyers turned to other exporters such as Thailand and Vietnam. International rice prices climbed in the months that followed.

A weak monsoon also affects water beyond the farm. Lower rainfall reduces reservoir storage and slows the recharge of groundwater. That puts pressure on drinking water supplies and on hydropower output in the dry months before the next monsoon.

Zambia felt the 2023–24 El Niño through a severe drought that spread across southern Africa. The government declared the drought a national disaster in early 2024, and low water in the Zambezi basin cut hydropower generation at Kariba.

Southern Africa's main rainy season runs roughly from November to April. El Niño tends to suppress rainfall across the region during those months. In Zambia, the dry spell struck during the growing season, when crops depended most on rain.

President Hakainde Hichilema made the disaster declaration. The step allows a government to redirect public funds and appeal for outside assistance. Neighboring Zimbabwe and Malawi also declared disasters as the drought deepened across the region.

Maize is Zambia's staple crop. It is the base of nshima, the stiff porridge served at most meals. Most Zambian farmers work small plots and rely on rainfall rather than irrigation. That leaves harvests exposed when the rains fail. The drought damaged crops in many farming areas.

The second blow fell on electricity. Zambia generates the large majority of its power from hydroelectric plants. The biggest of these draws on Lake Kariba, the reservoir behind Kariba Dam on the Zambezi River.

Kariba Dam was completed in the late 1950s and straddles the border with Zimbabwe. The two countries manage the reservoir jointly through the Zambezi River Authority. Power stations on each bank draw from the same body of water.

Weak inflows during the drought left less water available for generation. The Zambezi River Authority restricted how much water the power stations could use. ZESCO, Zambia's state-owned utility, responded with prolonged load-shedding. Households and businesses went without power for many hours a day.

The shortages reached beyond homes. Copper is Zambia's main export, and its mines are among the country's largest electricity users. Small businesses that depend on grid power, from welders to barbers, also lost working hours.

Zambia relies on rainfall for both its staple food and most of its electricity. During the 2023–24 drought, that dependence meant one poor rainy season strained the food supply and the power grid at the same time.

Kenya tends to receive heavier-than-normal short rains during El Niño years. That rainy season runs from October to December. In strong events it has brought widespread flooding, including in 1997–98 and again in late 2023.

Kenya has two main rainy seasons. The long rains fall roughly from March to May. The short rains arrive later in the year. El Niño's clearest signal in East Africa shows up in the second of these.

Farmers and herders plan around both seasons. A shift in the short rains has direct consequences for planting and grazing.

The 1997–98 episode showed how severe the impact can be. Rains far above normal fell across much of East Africa in late 1997. Rivers burst their banks, and roads and bridges washed out.

The standing floodwater also created breeding grounds for mosquitoes. An outbreak of Rift Valley fever followed in northeastern Kenya and southern Somalia. The disease affects both livestock and people.

Late 2023 repeated parts of that pattern. Heavy rains struck Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia during the short-rains season. Northeastern Kenya, including counties along the Tana River, saw extensive flooding. Many families were displaced from their homes.

The Indian Ocean plays a role too. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole — warmer water in the western Indian Ocean relative to the east — also tends to boost East African short rains. Both conditions were in place in late 2023. That overlap makes it inaccurate to credit El Niño alone for those floods.

The 2023 rains also arrived at a difficult moment. They followed a drought that spanned five consecutive failed rainy seasons across the Horn of Africa. Dry, hardened soil absorbs water poorly. Heavy rain on that ground tends to run off rather than soak in. Pastoralists who had already lost livestock to drought then faced floods.

La Niña tends to push the short rains the other way. The consecutive La Niña years from 2020 to 2023 were associated with that drought. For Kenya, the full ENSO cycle can mean swinging between too little rain and too much within a few years.

#5475. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 8:51 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

#5474. McDonald's is testing new value bundles as U.S. restaurant traffic slips

Free daily briefing on global business news.

U.S. comparable sales fell 0.2% in the third quarter as the chain tests two formats for a rollout set for early 2027

McDonald's $MCD is testing two new value menu formats at U.S. restaurants, CEO Chris Kempczinski said on the company's earnings call Wednesday.

The company reported third-quarter results on Wednesday showing U.S. comparable sales fell 0.2%, as negative comparable guest counts were mostly offset by positive check growth. Global comparable sales rose 1.5%. McDonald's stock finished Wednesday up by over 6%.

One format uses mix-and-match combinations, and the other uses fixed bundles of set items, according to MarketWatch. The eight-week test runs in about 1,900 locations spread over a few U.S. regions. The format that ends up winning over both franchisees and shoppers will go national in early 2027, according to CNBC.

"In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," Kempczinski said in a statement.

Chief Financial Officer Ian Borden said on the call that same-store sales rebounded in September, having declined through July and August, according to CNBC. Borden added that he had not claimed the fourth quarter would bring better U.S. same-store sales.

To address the decline, McDonald's put its marketing weight behind Extra Value Meals and revived promotions, both regional and nationwide, in its mobile app. Promotions have also featured breakfast sandwiches at $2 and complimentary fries for purchases of at least $1, according to Reuters.

According to Reuters, citing Placer.ai data, the number of customers visiting McDonald's restaurants dropped 4.6% in the third quarter compared with a year before. This was the first drop in U.S. comparable sales following a five-quarter run of increases.

Franchisee participation has been an issue. Executives said in August that a third of franchisees did not take part in the under-$3 menu, which hurt its execution. Kempczinski said the corporate side and U.S. franchisees are "in a good spot with the exception of this entry-level value."

The test follows a second quarter in which same-store sales grew 0.8% as guest counts declined. McDonald's outlined an $8.5 billion franchisee support package at an investor day in September, and U.S. executives acknowledged falling short on consistent execution. Skye Anderson became president of McDonald's USA in August.

Over the past two years, McDonald's has introduced a menu of items priced under $3 and a $4 breakfast meal.

#5473. Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor, whose app runs several coding agents at once

Meta Platforms Inc. has acquired artificial intelligence coding startup Conductor in a deal first reported today by Axios.

Conductor confirmed it’s joining Meta in a post on its website. Terms were not disclosed.

The company’s software lets a developer run several coding agents at once, each in an isolated copy of the codebase, and then review and merge what they produce. Supported agents include Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s Cursor, and users pay for them through their own subscriptions and keys.

The desktop app runs on Macs. A hosted version, Conductor Cloud, puts agents in sandboxed virtual machines where they can keep working for hours, and users can check on them from an iPhone app.

Engineers at Meta were using Conductor well before the deal. When the startup announced its Series A in March, it named Meta, Google LLC and Spotify Technology SA among the companies with dozens of engineers on the product. Conductor now says on its website that more than 100,000 people use it.

People familiar with the deal told Axios that Meta expects the Conductor team’s speed at shipping products to help it build its next generation of AI coding tools. The acquisition follows two Meta model releases last month that both pitched coding as a strength.

On Oct. 15, Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weights version of its Muse Spark model aimed at coding and long-running agent work. Meta’s more capable Muse Wonder models stay closed inside its own Muse Code terminal and application programming interface.

The Conductor deal landed the same day OpenAI said it plans to acquire developer tools startup Pierre Computer. OpenAI had already announced plans in June to buy Ona, which runs coding agents in cloud sandboxes.

Local copies of the Mac app keep working until early 2027, when the team expects to release a new interface it has not yet described. New models and critical bug fixes stop arriving at that point, and Conductor will delete the app’s user data. The company said it has never sold Conductor user data or trained models on it, and does not plan to.

Chief Executive Charlie Holtz and Chief Technology Officer Jackson de Campos founded the company, formally Melty Inc., in 2024. Conductor raised a $22 million Series A in March from Spark Capital and Matrix. Y Combinator and the founders of Notion and Linear are also backers.

#5472. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.

#5471. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5470. Arm Holdings beat revenue expectations thanks to data center demand

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Revenue rose 27% to $1.44 billion, a record for a second quarter, as license revenue climbed 50% and royalty revenue rose 8%

Arm Holdings reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $1.44 billion on Wednesday, up 27% year over year and a record for a second quarter. License and other revenue totaled $773 million, a 50% increase, and royalty revenue came in at $670 million, up 8%.

Non-GAAP earnings were $0.52 a share, compared with $0.39 in the year-ago period. Wall Street had forecast sales of $1.38 billion and per-share earnings of 47 cents, according to Bloomberg.

Royalty growth came from higher royalty rates per chip, such as Armv9 architecture and Arm CSS, and from more Arm-based chips deployed in data centers, the company said. Memory pricing's effect on the smartphone market partly offset those gains. License revenue growth was driven by demand for Arm technology, the timing and size of multiple high-value license agreements, and contributions from backlog, the company said.

Spending by data center operators and the vendors that supply them on licenses and chip designs from Arm has grown, making up for weakness in the smartphone business.

GAAP net income was $130 million, or $0.12 a share, compared with $0.22 a share in the year-ago period. Non-GAAP operating margin rose to 44.2% from 41.1%, and annualized contract value increased 12% to $1.79 billion.

Arm expects fiscal third-quarter revenue of about $1.54 billion, the company said. Analysts had averaged a forecast of $1.53 billion.

CEO Rene Haas said the company has more confidence in reaching its revenue target for its new data center chip, according to Bloomberg. Arm expects revenue from the chip to reach as much as $2 billion across fiscal 2027 and 2028.

"We could probably do more if we had more supply," Haas said. "We're signaling strong confidence in achieving that number."

The chip is the AGI CPU, Arm's first in-house central processing unit built for data centers. Arm said in May it saw a path to $2 billion in demand for the chip, twice what it had projected at the chip's March unveiling. The open question has been whether Arm can secure enough manufacturing capacity, as chipmakers compete for limited production capacity during the AI spending boom.

Arm stock barely moved in after-hours trading following the results. It had risen over 75% so far in the year, measured at Wednesday's close.

#5469. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

#5468. Qualcomm's push into new markets drives a sales forecast that beats expectations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Qualcomm's earnings-per-share outlook came in below analyst expectations, and its stock fell about 5% in extended trading

Qualcomm $QCOM reported fiscal fourth-quarter results on Wednesday and forecast revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion for the current quarter, a range that includes its data center business.

The company guided to non-GAAP earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 a share. Analysts had projected revenue of $10.55 billion, according to Bloomberg. The midpoint of the earnings range landed below the average analyst estimate of $2.32 a share. Qualcomm stock dropped roughly 5% in after-hours trading.

For the quarter ended Sept. 27, Qualcomm's GAAP revenue fell 8% to $10.3 billion. Non-GAAP earnings were $2.17 a share, down 28% from a year earlier. Analysts had forecast $10.1 billion in revenue and per-share earnings of $2.16.

Handset revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion. Automotive revenue rose 89% to a record $1.99 billion, and revenue from internet-of-things products rose 4% to $1.89 billion. Analysts had projected handset revenue of $5.25 billion, according to Bloomberg, which said the automotive and internet-of-things figures beat estimates.

"We are pleased to deliver fourth quarter non-GAAP revenues at the high end of our guidance," CEO Cristiano Amon said in a statement. Amon said non-handset revenue is projected to grow more than 60% in fiscal 2027, and the company reiterated its fiscal 2027 data center revenue target of $5 billion.

Qualcomm said the semiconductor industry is facing a broad increase in input costs across wafer fabrication, assembly, test, advanced packaging, memory and other materials. The company said it is raising product prices to reflect the higher costs and expects the full benefit in chip-segment gross margins in the second half of fiscal 2027.

For all of fiscal 2026, Qualcomm reported GAAP revenue of $43.1 billion, down 3%, and non-GAAP earnings of $10.54 a share, down 12%. The company also said it renewed long-term patent license agreements with Apple $AAPL, Huawei and Transsion and announced a multi-generational product collaboration with Amazon $AMZN for AI data centers.

Qualcomm raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset revenue target to $40 billion at its investor day in June. That plan includes a data center revenue target of more than $15 billion, along with $10 billion in automotive revenue and more than $14 billion in internet-of-things revenue.

At the same event, Qualcomm said Meta $META Platforms would use its Dragonfly C1000 server processors, which are expected to be available in 2028. Qualcomm also agreed to acquire AI software startup Modular in an all-stock deal valued at $3.92 billion.

#5467. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5466. Cyber ups and downs: Datadog falls 14% on outlook tied to one customer as Rapid7 jumps and Fastly slides

Datadog Inc., Rapid7 Inc. and Fastly Inc. all beat Wall Street’s third-quarter forecasts today, but Rapid7 was the only one of the three to see its shares rise.

A cautious outlook tied to one large customer knocked about 14% off Datadog’s stock in regular trading. Rapid7 jumped 18% after hours on results that came despite a decline in revenue.

For its third quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Datadog reported adjusted earnings of 81 cents per share, up from 55 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 64 cents per share on revenue of $1.14 billion.

Unadjusted net income climbed to $118.3 million from $33.9 million, and the adjusted operating margin widened five points to 28%. Billings in the quarter rose 30% to $1.16 billion, Chief Financial Officer David Obstler said on the earnings call, with remaining performance obligations up 38% at $3.85 billion. Free cash flow came to $251 million.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Olivier Pomel told analysts that more than 850 artificial intelligence companies now use Datadog, roughly 100 more than at the end of June. Adoption is strong across the platform as customers scale “their digital operations and use of AI,” he said in the earnings release. Customers worth $100,000 or more a year in recurring revenue rose 20% to about 4,860.

Full-year guidance went up. Datadog now expects 2026 revenue of $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion, against the $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion it projected in August, and adjusted earnings of $2.73 to $2.75 per share. Fourth-quarter adjusted earnings are forecast at 69 to 71 cents per share.

Revenue for the fourth quarter is guided at $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly what analysts had expected, with the top of the range only about $3 million above third-quarter revenue. The forecast assumes Datadog’s largest customer, an AI provider the company has not named, spends no more than its contractual minimum, according to Obstler.

Usage on that account dropped in the third quarter while staying above the floor. Excluding it, implied fourth-quarter growth is in the low- to mid-30% range. Early renewals with some large AI customers, signed at higher commitments in return for better pricing, are also holding back near-term revenue.

The roughly 14% drop today made it two straight quarters in which a beat failed to hold up the stock. Datadog shares closed 19% lower in August, the day the company disclosed the customer’s planned cutback.

In Rapid7’s third quarter, also ended Sept. 30, the cybersecurity company posted adjusted earnings of 60 cents per share, up from 57 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $212.4 million, down 2.5% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 46 cents per share on revenue of $209 million.

Annualized recurring revenue slipped 2.2%, to $819.7 million, ahead of the roughly $812 million the company had guided to in August. Adjusted operating income rose to $46.2 million from $36.9 million. Unadjusted net income fell to $3.5 million from $9.8 million after $10 million in restructuring costs from the 12% workforce cut announced in August and a $5.5 million write-down on a strategic equity investment.

Rapid7 demonstrated its Agentic SOC at Black Hat USA in August, using AI agents to speed up investigations while leaving high-impact decisions to analysts. Wael Mohamed, who took over as CEO in June, said the core business “is becoming more stable” and that “one quarter of stability is just a start.” Rapid7 is “not declaring victory,” he added.

The company’s full-year adjusted earnings forecast moved to $1.94 to $1.96 per share, well above the $1.78 to $1.83 it gave three months ago. Revenue guidance edged up to $841 million to $843 million. For the fourth quarter, Rapid7 sees revenue of $208 million to $210 million, down 3% to 4% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of 53 to 55 cents per share.

The stock climbed about 18% in extended trading.

Edge cloud platform provider Fastly reported adjusted earnings of 17 cents per share for its third quarter, up from 7 cents a year earlier, on record revenue of $190.2 million, up 20% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 12 cents per share on revenue of $187.9 million.

Most of Fastly’s revenue still comes from network services, which grew 16%, to $138 million. Security sales rose twice as fast, to $44.7 million, in a quarter when the company also launched AI Firewall to block prompt injection and other attacks before they reach a model. Trailing-12-month net retention was its highest since 2022, at 119%. The top 10 customers now account for 39% of revenue, up from 32% a year ago.

Fourth-quarter revenue is forecast at $198 million to $202 million, ahead of the $197 million analysts had modeled. Full-year revenue guidance moved up to $744 million to $748 million from $732 million to $746 million in August. Adjusted earnings for 2026 are now expected at 61 to 63 cents per share. None of that stopped Fastly shares from falling about 14% after the bell.

#5465. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.
