#5464. How the British royal family makes its money: 10 sources and mechanisms

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A guide to how the royal family makes money through 10 funding sources and mechanisms, from the Sovereign Grant and Crown Estate to two duchies and voluntary taxes

The British monarchy's public funding is pegged to the profits of a property business the king does not personally own. Its private income comes from landed estates, one of which was created in 1337. Following the money means following both tracks, plus costs that other parts of government cover.

Any explanation of how the royal family makes money starts with a split between public and private funds. The public side is the Sovereign Grant. It pays for official duties, royal household staff and the upkeep of occupied royal palaces. Since the Sovereign Grant Act 2011 took effect in 2012, the grant has been calculated as a share of Crown Estate profits from two years earlier. It is not a fixed sum voted by Parliament each year. The private side includes income from the Duchy of Lancaster, which goes to the monarch. It also includes the Duchy of Cornwall, whose income goes to the heir to the throne.

A second distinction separates property held by the office from property owned by the person. The Crown Estate belongs to the reigning monarch by virtue of the throne. Its holdings include Regent Street in London and much of the seabed around England, Wales and Northern Ireland. A commercial organization runs it independently, and its profits go to the Treasury. The Royal Collection is held in trust for future sovereigns and the nation. Balmoral in Scotland and Sandringham in Norfolk are different. The monarch owns them privately, and their upkeep comes from private funds.

A third layer covers costs and obligations that never pass through royal accounts. Security for the royal family is paid from government and police budgets. Some costs of state occasions are met by government departments. Since 1993, the monarch has paid income tax and capital gains tax on private income under a voluntary arrangement. A separate 1993 agreement exempts assets passed from one sovereign to the next from inheritance tax.

In 1760, George III gave up the hereditary revenues of the Crown in exchange for a fixed payment known as the Civil List. That system lasted until 2012. The 10 slides that follow explain a selection of sources and mechanisms behind royal finances, not a complete ledger. Each one sets out how a single piece works, who receives the money and where the public and private boundaries fall.

The Sovereign Grant is the main source of public money for the British monarchy. It pays for the monarch's official duties, the staff who carry out that work and the upkeep of the royal palaces that are in use.

Parliament does not vote on a fresh sum for the grant each year. A formula sets the amount instead. That formula makes the grant a share of the profits earned by the Crown Estate, the property portfolio attached to the office of monarch.

The monarch does not collect those profits directly. They are paid to the Treasury. The grant is public money whose size is set by reference to those profits.

The calculation uses a profit figure from two years earlier. The grant paid in any year is therefore based on how the Crown Estate performed two years before. It does not track the estate's results in the year the money is spent.

The Sovereign Grant Act 2011 created this formula. It took effect in 2012.

The percentage of profits used in the formula is not fixed for all time. It has been changed since 2011. The size of the grant can therefore move for two separate reasons. One is a revision to that percentage. The other is a change in the Crown Estate's profits.

The grant's purpose is narrower than the phrase "royal money" might suggest. It is meant for the official side of the monarchy — the work the sovereign does as head of state, and the buildings and people needed to support it. It does not pay for the monarch's privately owned homes. It is also not a personal salary for the monarch or the wider family.

Costs that fall outside the grant's scope are met from other sources. These include private income held by the monarch, which pays for expenses the public grant does not cover.

The Crown Estate is a property portfolio whose profits go to the Treasury, not to the monarch. It belongs to whoever is reigning, by virtue of the office of sovereign. The king does not own it as personal property and cannot treat its earnings as private income.

The portfolio is run independently as a commercial business. The monarch does not manage it. Its legal framework is the Crown Estate Act 1961, the statute that governs how the estate operates.

Its holdings mix city property with natural resources. In London, the estate owns Regent Street, the West End shopping thoroughfare. Offshore, it holds much of the seabed around England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

That seabed produces income through offshore wind leasing. Developers who want to build wind farms in those waters lease seabed rights from the estate. The income from those leases adds to the estate's overall profits, alongside earnings from its property holdings.

The path those profits follow is what links the Crown Estate to royal funding. The money passes to the Treasury, where it becomes part of government revenue. A share then comes back to the monarchy through the Sovereign Grant, the main public payment to the royal household.

The connection is indirect. The monarchy's public funding is tied to how the Crown Estate performs. Even so, the monarch never collects the estate's profits. The amount returned depends on the share set for the Sovereign Grant, not on any personal claim to the earnings.

The arrangement also keeps the estate apart from the royal family's private wealth. The Duchy of Lancaster and the Duchy of Cornwall operate separately from it. So do Balmoral and Sandringham, which the monarch owns privately. When the throne passes to a new monarch, the Crown Estate passes with the office. It was never the outgoing sovereign's to keep.

The Duchy of Lancaster is a private estate that gives the reigning monarch an income outside the public funding system. That income, known as the Privy Purse, pays for expenses the Sovereign Grant does not cover.

The monarch holds the duchy under the title Duke $DUK of Lancaster. The estate belongs to whoever reigns, and it passes to each new sovereign with the crown.

The duchy's holdings include farmland and commercial property. The income they produce goes to the monarch rather than to the Treasury.

That flow of money separates the duchy from the Crown Estate. Crown Estate profits go to the Treasury, and the monarchy gets a share back only through the Sovereign Grant. Duchy of Lancaster income reaches the monarch directly.

The Privy Purse covers spending that falls outside the grant's categories of official duties, palace upkeep and household staff. Some of that spending supports relatives. The Privy Purse meets some costs of other working members of the royal family.

Privy Purse income counts as private income for tax purposes. It falls under the voluntary arrangement through which the monarch pays tax on private income.

The Duchy of Cornwall is a private estate whose income goes to the heir to the throne, who also holds the title Duke $DUK of Cornwall. Prince William has held that title, and received the duchy's income, since Sept. 8, 2022.

That was the day his father, Charles, became king. The dukedom passed from father to son on the same date the throne changed hands.

Edward III created the duchy in 1337 for his son, the Black Prince. The estate was tied to the heir from the start. That link still decides who benefits from it nearly seven centuries later.

The title and the income move together. Whoever holds the dukedom receives the duchy's revenue. The reigning monarch does not. A king or queen draws private income from a different estate, the Duchy of Lancaster.

The duchy's holdings reach into London. It owns the Oval cricket ground in Kennington and leases the ground to Surrey. That lease makes the duchy the landlord of the county cricket club's home ground.

The duchy also owns the land under Poundbury, a town development in Dorset. Construction there began in 1993. The development sits on duchy land, and the duchy's income goes to the heir.

The duchy is not liable for corporation tax. The heir pays income tax on the duchy's income on a voluntary basis instead.

Balmoral Castle in Scotland and Sandringham House in Norfolk are owned privately by the monarch. Their running costs come from private money, and the Sovereign Grant does not pay for their upkeep.

That status sets them apart from the best-known royal residences. Buckingham Palace and Windsor Castle are tied to the office of sovereign rather than to the person who holds it. As occupied palaces, they receive maintenance funding through the Sovereign Grant. Balmoral and Sandringham receive none.

Both estates came into the family through private purchases in the 19th century. Prince Albert bought Balmoral for Queen Victoria. The castle that stands there today was built for the couple. Sandringham was bought for Victoria's eldest son, the future Edward VII, while he was Prince of Wales. Neither property became part of the public estate.

Balmoral sits in Aberdeenshire, inside Cairngorms National Park. It has long served as the royal family's summer retreat. Queen Elizabeth II died there on Sept. 8, 2022. Sandringham lies in northwest Norfolk. It is where the royal family traditionally gathers at Christmas.

Neither house stands alone. Each sits at the center of a working rural estate with farmland, woodland and tenants. Parts of Sandringham House and its grounds open to paying visitors for part of the year. Balmoral's grounds also open to the public on a seasonal basis. Money from that land and those visitors is private estate income. It does not go to the Treasury.

Private ownership also means the two estates follow the person, not the office. When Charles became king in 2022, Balmoral and Sandringham became his personal property. The occupied palaces, by contrast, come with the throne itself.

For readers asking who pays for the royal family, Balmoral and Sandringham mark the line between public and private money. The palaces used for official work draw on public funding through the grant. These two country estates belong to the monarch personally, and the monarch covers their costs.

Ticket sales at royal sites earn money for the Royal Collection Trust, a registered charity, not for the royal family. The trust spends that income on conserving and displaying the Royal Collection.

The Royal Collection is not the monarch's personal property. The sovereign holds it in trust for future monarchs and for the nation. A king cannot treat it as a private asset that produces income for himself.

The trust charges admission at royal sites, including the State Rooms at Buckingham Palace and Windsor Castle. The money from those tickets stays inside the charity.

That income pays for two kinds of work. Conservation keeps objects in the collection in good condition. Display puts those objects in front of visitors.

Charitable status keeps the trust's finances apart from the royal household's. Admission revenue is not part of the Sovereign Grant. It does not go to members of the royal family.

The same split runs through the palaces themselves. The Sovereign Grant covers the upkeep of occupied royal palaces as working buildings. The objects shown in their State Rooms are a separate matter, and their care is funded through the trust.

For anyone asking who pays for the royal family, this arrangement shows that some money linked to royal sites never reaches the royals. A visitor who buys a ticket to the State Rooms at Windsor Castle is paying for the care and display of the collection, not for the household's running costs.

The British monarch has paid income tax and capital gains tax on private income since 1993. No law requires the payments. They are made voluntarily, and the arrangement has continued from Queen Elizabeth II's reign into King Charles III's.

Before 1993, the sovereign paid no income tax. Elizabeth II started paying that year and kept doing so for the rest of her reign, which ended with her death on Sept. 8, 2022. Charles, who became king that day, already paid income tax voluntarily on his own private income while he was heir. He has carried the practice on as monarch.

Two taxes fall under the arrangement. Income tax applies to the private money the monarch receives each year. Capital gains tax applies to profits made when private assets are sold. In both cases, the sovereign pays because of the voluntary agreement, not because a statute compels it. The payments go to HM Revenue and Customs, the U.K. tax authority.

The Privy Purse is one of the income streams the agreement reaches. The term refers to the income of the Duchy of Lancaster, a private estate the monarch holds as Duke $DUK of Lancaster. It covers spending that falls outside the Sovereign Grant, including some costs of other working members of the royal family. Privy Purse receipts are dealt with under the voluntary tax agreement.

The Sovereign Grant sits on the other side of the line. It is public money for the monarch's official role, and it is not treated as taxable income. That split mirrors the wider division in royal finances between what belongs to the office and what belongs to the person who holds it.

The heir to the throne follows a similar practice. Income from the Duchy of Cornwall goes to the heir, who pays income tax on it voluntarily. Prince William has held the duchy since his father became king in 2022.

Assets that pass from one British monarch to the next are exempt from inheritance tax. The exemption comes from a 1993 agreement and is tied to the succession, not to the royal family as a group.

Inheritance tax is the U.K. charge on what a person leaves behind at death. Under the 1993 arrangement, property moving from a monarch to the succeeding monarch does not trigger that charge. The recipient decides the outcome. The same asset can be exempt or taxable depending on whether it goes to the new sovereign or to someone else.

The scope is narrow. Gifts and bequests outside the sovereign-to-sovereign route follow the ordinary rules that apply to everyone else. A monarch who leaves assets to a child who is not the next sovereign, or to another relative, does not benefit from the exemption. Gifts made between other members of the family are treated the same way.

The most recent change of monarch came on Sept. 8, 2022, when Charles became king after the death of Queen Elizabeth II. That handover is the kind of transfer the sovereign-to-sovereign rule covers.

The exemption concerns what a monarch owns personally. Holdings tied to the office pass with the throne regardless of any tax agreement. The Crown Estate and the Royal Collection are two examples. The 1993 agreement does not govern them. It deals with assets a sovereign owns privately.

For royal finances, the effect is that a monarch's private wealth can reach the successor without the reduction an ordinary estate would face at death.

Royal security is not paid for out of the Sovereign Grant. Protection for members of the British royal family is funded from government and police budgets instead.

That puts the cost of guarding the royals on the state's books, not the royal household's. The grant covers the monarchy's official work. Protecting the people who carry out that work is treated as a separate public responsibility.

The arrangement also keeps security outside the formula that sets the grant. A change in what protection costs does not change the amount the royal household receives. A change in the grant does not change the protection budget either.

A similar split applies to parts of national ceremonial life. Government departments meet some of the costs of state occasions. The monarch stands at the center of these events, but part of the bill sits in departmental budgets rather than in the grant.

The split shapes any answer to the question of who pays for the royal family. A tally built only from the Sovereign Grant shows what the household spends from its main public payment. It leaves out security and the state occasion costs held elsewhere.

Public money linked to the monarchy therefore runs in two streams. One is the grant, paid to the monarchy and spent by the royal household. The other is spending by government departments and the police. That spending supports the monarchy's work without passing through royal accounts.

Royal funding moved from the Civil List, a fixed payment created under George III in 1760, to the Sovereign Grant in 2012. The newer system ties the monarchy's public funding to the profits of the Crown Estate rather than to a set sum.

The Civil List grew out of a trade. In 1760, George III handed the hereditary revenues of the Crown to the government. In return, he received a fixed payment to support the monarchy.

Under that deal, the money the Crown's revenues produced went to the government. The king and his successors relied on the agreed payment instead.

A fixed payment works differently from a share. Its value did not move up or down with the income from the revenues the king had surrendered. The payment and the revenues followed separate paths.

The arrangement lasted more than 250 years. The Sovereign Grant Act 2011, passed by Parliament, brought it to an end. The new law took effect in 2012. From that year, the Sovereign Grant replaced the Civil List.

The central change was the link between royal funding and the Crown Estate. Public money for the monarchy is no longer set as a fixed payment. It is calculated as a share of Crown Estate profits.

The profits themselves still do not go to the monarch. They are paid to the Treasury. A portion then returns to the monarchy in the form of the Sovereign Grant.

That portion has not stayed the same. The percentage used in the calculation has changed since the 2011 act was passed.

Both systems answer one question: how the state pays for the monarchy's official role. They differ in how the amount is set. Under the Civil List, the sum was fixed. Under the Sovereign Grant, it follows the profits of a property portfolio held by the Crown.

#5463. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5462. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5461. 10 royals with vast fortunes and the assets behind them

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A look at 10 wealthy royals around the world and the crown estates, oil economies, banks and holding companies tied to their ruling families

Royal wealth is rarely audited and almost never disclosed in full. That makes any single dollar figure attached to a king, sultan or emir an estimate. Published estimates for the same person also differ from one outlet to the next and from one year to the next. A more useful question is what each family controls, and through which structures.

The answer changes sharply by country. In some Gulf monarchies, the ruling family sits at the head of a state built on oil and gas revenue. There, the line between the treasury and the palace is often unclear or undocumented. Large sovereign wealth funds in the region belong to governments, even when members of the ruling family run or oversee them. In constitutional monarchies such as the U.K., the separation is spelled out in law. Some assets belong to the crown as an institution. Others produce private income for the monarch and the heir.

Other royal fortunes run through named institutions and companies. Thailand's royal holdings are managed by the Crown Property Bureau. A 2018 law put those assets under the king's personal control. Morocco's royal family is linked to Al Mada, a holding company with interests across several sectors of the national economy. Liechtenstein's princely family owns LGT Group, which provides private banking and asset management. Brunei's sultan presides over an oil and gas economy and lives in a palace with 1,788 rooms.

This article presents a selection of 10, not a ranking. Each slide covers a different monarch or ruling family, from Bangkok to Monaco. The mechanisms run from crown property and royal duchies to state oil companies, sovereign funds and private banking. Together they show how wealthy royals around the world hold and manage assets, and where those assets end and the state's begin.

Where reliable numbers do not exist, this list leaves them out. The order of the slides carries no meaning about relative wealth. The focus stays on what can be verified: who rules, since when and which institutions sit behind the throne.

King Maha Vajiralongkorn of Thailand personally controls the royal holdings managed by the Crown Property Bureau. Under legislation passed in 2018, those assets became his own rather than property of the monarchy as an institution.

He took the throne in 2016 after the death of his father, King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who had reigned since 1946. His coronation was held in May 2019 in Bangkok. The ceremonies ran over several days and drew on Buddhist and Brahmin ritual.

Vajiralongkorn is the 10th king of the Chakri dynasty and is also known as Rama X $TWTR. King Rama I founded the dynasty in 1782 and moved the capital to Bangkok. Siam, as Thailand was then called, became a constitutional monarchy after a 1932 revolution ended absolute royal rule.

The Crown Property Bureau was created in the 1930s to manage assets linked to the throne. Thai law at the time sorted royal-related wealth into three categories. These were the king's private property, state property used by the monarchy, and crown property, which belonged to the monarchy as an institution.

For decades, the finance minister chaired the bureau's board. That arrangement tied the royal portfolio to the government, even though the assets were not state property.

The bureau's holdings include large areas of land in central Bangkok. Much of that land is leased to businesses, government agencies and residents. The portfolio has also long included major stakes in Siam Cement Group, an industrial conglomerate, and Siam Commercial Bank, one of the country's oldest lenders.

The 2018 change erased the old line between crown property and the king's personal wealth for these holdings. Shareholdings once listed under the bureau were then registered in the king's name.

The shift made Vajiralongkorn the direct owner of assets that earlier monarchs did not hold personally. No audited valuation of the portfolio is published. The bureau does not release full accounts to the public.

King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has led Saudi Arabia since January 2015. His family, the House of Saud, rules a kingdom whose economy rests on oil. How much of that wealth belongs personally to the royals, rather than to the state, is not publicly documented.

Salman became king after the death of his half-brother, King Abdullah. He is one of the sons of King Abdulaziz, known as Ibn Saud, who founded the modern Saudi state in 1932. Since Abdulaziz died in 1953, the crown has passed among his sons.

Before taking the throne, Salman spent decades as governor of Riyadh province. He became defense minister in 2011 and crown prince in 2012. That long administrative career made him one of the most senior figures in the family well before his accession.

Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy. The king is head of state, and the country has no elected national legislature. In 2017, Salman named his son Mohammed bin Salman crown prince. In 2022, the crown prince also became prime minister, a post the king had previously held.

Oil defines the kingdom's finances. Commercial quantities were discovered in the late 1930s, and the industry grew under American oil companies. The Saudi government took full ownership of that operation over the following decades, and it became Saudi Aramco. The state remains its majority owner. In December 2019, the government listed a small portion of its shares on the Riyadh stock exchange.

That structure explains why estimates of Saudi royal wealth are hard to pin down. Oil revenue flows to the state, and the royal family governs the state. No public accounting separates the family's private holdings from national assets. Any single figure for the House of Saud's fortune rests on that unresolved boundary.

The family is also large. It includes thousands of members descended from Abdulaziz and his relatives. Many hold government posts, business interests or both. Those individual fortunes vary widely and are not disclosed.

The kingdom's economic planning now looks beyond crude. The Vision 2030 program, announced in 2016 under Mohammed bin Salman, aims to diversify the economy away from oil. The Public Investment Fund, the state's sovereign wealth fund, is a central vehicle for that effort.

Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah has ruled Brunei since 1967, and his wealth comes from the small state's oil and gas. He is also Brunei's prime minister. That makes him both head of state and head of government.

He became sultan in October 1967, when his father, Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III, abdicated. His coronation took place the following year. He is the 29th sultan in a royal line that traces its origins back more than six centuries. In 2017, Brunei marked his Golden Jubilee, 50 years on the throne.

The premiership is only one of his cabinet posts. He also holds the defense and finance portfolios. Brunei has no elected legislature. Its Legislative Council is appointed. The state's official ideology, Melayu Islam Beraja, or Malay Islamic Monarchy, places the throne at the center of national life.

Hydrocarbons underpin the economy. Oil was discovered at Seria in 1929. Crude oil and liquefied natural gas remain the country's main exports. Brunei Shell $SHEL Petroleum, a joint venture between the government and Shell, runs much of the oil and gas production. The Brunei Investment Agency manages the state's overseas reserves. Brunei does not publish an accounting that separates the sultan's personal assets from those state holdings.

The Istana Nurul Iman is his official residence. It stands on the bank of the Brunei River in Bandar Seri Begawan, the capital. Guinness World Records lists it as the world's largest residential palace. The Filipino architect Leandro Locsin designed it. Its throne hall is used for state ceremonies.

The palace was completed in 1984, the same year Brunei became independent from the U.K. Independence ended nearly a century of Brunei's status as a British protectorate.

The palace also opens to the public once a year. At the end of Ramadan, it holds an open house for Hari Raya Aidilfitri. During those days, the sultan and members of the royal family receive visitors in person.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan rules Abu Dhabi, the emirate that holds most of the UAE's oil. He became president of the UAE in May 2022, after the death of his half-brother Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed.

He is a son of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. His father led the founding of the UAE federation in 1971 and served as its first president. The Al Nahyan family has ruled Abu Dhabi for generations.

The UAE is a federation of seven emirates, and each has its own ruler. The Federal Supreme Council, made up of those seven rulers, elects the president. The ruler of Abu Dhabi has held the presidency since the federation began.

Sheikh Mohammed spent nearly two decades as crown prince of Abu Dhabi before taking the top post. He was named crown prince in 2004. He trained at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in the U.K. and built his early career in the UAE armed forces.

Abu Dhabi is the largest of the seven emirates by area. It covers most of the country's land. The state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, known as ADNOC, runs the emirate's oil production.

Much of the emirate's surplus revenue goes into sovereign investment vehicles. The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, set up in 1976, invests government money across global markets. Mubadala, established in 2002, holds stakes in a range of industries. Its holdings include the chipmaker GlobalFoundries.

Neither fund is Sheikh Mohammed's private fortune. Both are government entities that invest on behalf of the emirate. As ruler, he heads the state that owns them. The assets themselves belong to Abu Dhabi, not to him personally.

His personal wealth has never been publicly disclosed. No public accounting separates the family's private holdings from the emirate's state assets.

Other members of the family hold major private assets of their own. His brother Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed bought the English football club Manchester City in 2008. He made the purchase through his investment company, Abu Dhabi United Group.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum has ruled Dubai since January 2006. He is also vice president and prime minister of the UAE. The emirate's best-known assets, including the airline Emirates, sit with government-owned entities rather than in a disclosed personal fortune.

He became ruler after the death of his elder brother, Sheikh Maktoum bin Rashid Al Maktoum. Their father, Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum, led Dubai before both of them. The Al Maktoum family has governed Dubai since 1833.

Dubai is one of seven emirates that make up the UAE, a federation formed in 1971. By long-standing practice, the ruler of Abu Dhabi holds the federal presidency and the ruler of Dubai holds the vice presidency. Sheikh Mohammed pairs that role with the post of prime minister. That puts him at the head of the federal cabinet.

Emirates shows how Dubai's largest businesses are structured. The airline is owned by the Investment Corporation of Dubai, the emirate's main investment arm. That body belongs to the Dubai government. Emirates is therefore a state asset, not the ruler's private property.

Dubai's economy has developed along different lines from Abu Dhabi's. Its own oil output is small. The emirate has leaned instead on trade, aviation, tourism, real estate and financial services. Emirates began flying in 1985. Its growth helped turn Dubai International Airport into a major hub for long-haul connecting traffic.

The ruler's personal holdings are far less documented than the state's. His best-known private venture is Godolphin, the thoroughbred racing and breeding operation he founded in 1992. Its horses race in Europe, the Middle East, Australia and other markets. No official figure for his personal net worth has been published.

His son, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum, was named crown prince of Dubai in 2008. He is next in line to rule the emirate. In July 2024, he was also appointed the UAE's deputy prime minister and minister of defense.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has been emir of Qatar since June 2013, when his father abdicated in his favor. His country's wealth comes mainly from natural gas. The largest pools of that wealth belong to the state, not to the ruler personally.

His father, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, had ruled since 1995. Voluntary handovers of power are rare among Gulf monarchies. Sheikh Tamim was born in 1980 and trained at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in the U.K. He served as deputy commander of the armed forces and headed the Qatar Olympic Committee before taking the throne.

The Al Thani family has governed the peninsula since the 19th century. Qatar gained independence from the U.K. in 1971. A constitution approved by referendum in 2003 makes the emir head of state. He appoints the prime minister and the cabinet. Qatar held its first elections to the Shura Council, its legislative body, in 2021.

The economic base is the North Field, an offshore gas reservoir in the Persian Gulf and one of the largest in the world. Iran shares the same formation and calls its portion South Pars. State-owned QatarEnergy, known as Qatar Petroleum until 2021, develops the field. It exports liquefied natural gas to buyers across Asia and Europe.

Gas revenue flows into the Qatar Investment Authority, the state's sovereign wealth fund, which was established in 2005. The fund is a state asset, not part of the emir's private estate. Its investments reach well beyond the Gulf. Qatar Holding, a subsidiary of the fund, bought the London department store Harrods in 2010.

That overseas activity has made Qatar a visible investor in property, finance and sport. The country hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup, the first held in the Arab world.

The emir's personal fortune is a separate matter, and it is not publicly disclosed. Qatar does not publish an accounting that divides the ruling family's private holdings from national assets. Any figure attached to Sheikh Tamim alone is an outside estimate, not an official number.

King Mohammed VI of Morocco has reigned since July 1999. His family is linked to Al Mada, a Casablanca-based holding company formerly known as SNI, with stakes in banking, mining, energy and telecoms.

Mohammed VI was born in Rabat in 1963. He came to the throne after the death of his father, King Hassan II, who had reigned since 1961. Both belong to the Alaouite dynasty, which has ruled Morocco since the 17th century. The king's constitutional titles include Commander of the Faithful, which gives him a religious role alongside a political one.

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy, but the king retains wide executive power. A new constitution approved by referendum in 2011 gave the elected prime minister and parliament more authority. The king kept control over the military, religious affairs and major strategic appointments.

Al Mada took shape through a series of mergers and name changes. SNI, short for Société Nationale d'Investissement, merged with the conglomerate Omnium Nord-Africain, known as ONA, in 2010. The combined group adopted the Al Mada name in 2018. Casablanca, where the group is based, is Morocco's commercial capital.

Banking is the best-known part of the portfolio. Al Mada holds a stake in Attijariwafa bank, one of Morocco's largest lenders. The bank also operates in a number of other African countries. The mining company Managem, which produces metals including cobalt and silver, belongs to the same group. So does Nareva, an energy company that develops wind farms. In telecoms, Al Mada holds a stake in the operator Inwi. Its retail interests have included the hypermarket chain Marjane. Attijariwafa bank and Managem both trade on the Casablanca Stock Exchange.

Al Mada is a privately held company, not a state investment fund.

The value of the royal family's holdings has not been officially published. The family's role in major companies has been a recurring subject of debate in Moroccan politics and media.

Prince Hans-Adam II of Liechtenstein heads a princely family that owns LGT Group, a private banking and asset management firm. He has been the reigning prince of the small Alpine state since 1989.

LGT is based in Vaduz, the capital of Liechtenstein. It manages wealth for private clients and institutional investors. The firm ties the princely house directly to financial services, a sector that plays a large role in the country's economy.

Hans-Adam was born in 1945. He studied business economics at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland. He succeeded his father, Prince Franz Joseph II, who died in November 1989.

In 2004, he handed day-to-day government duties to his son, Hereditary Prince Alois. Hans-Adam remains head of state. Alois exercises the sovereign's powers on his father's behalf.

Liechtenstein's monarch holds more political power than most of Europe's reigning royals. In a 2003 referendum, voters approved constitutional changes proposed by Hans-Adam that confirmed the prince's veto over legislation. The changes also gave the prince the power to dismiss the government.

Voters returned to the question in 2012. They rejected a proposal that would have stripped the prince of his power to veto the results of referendums.

The principality sits between Switzerland and Austria. It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, along with Uzbekistan. Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc as its currency.

The family's history predates the country. Its name comes from Liechtenstein Castle in Lower Austria. The principality was created in 1719, when Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI combined the lordship of Schellenberg and the county of Vaduz.

Beyond banking, the princely family holds the Princely Collections, a private art collection that includes works by Peter Paul Rubens. Pieces from the collection are displayed at the Liechtenstein Garden Palace in Vienna.

The family lives at Vaduz Castle, which overlooks the capital. It does not publish a total value for its holdings.

King Charles III receives his private income from the Duchy of Lancaster, an estate held by the reigning British monarch since 1399. The Duchy of Cornwall is the other main income-producing estate tied to the monarchy. It now provides income to his heir.

Charles acceded in September 2022 after the death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II. His coronation took place at Westminster Abbey in May 2023. Before that, he was the longest-serving heir apparent in British history.

The Duchy of Lancaster is a portfolio of land, property and financial investments, mostly in England and Wales. Its net income goes to the monarch and is known as the Privy Purse. The sovereign holds the title Duke $DUK of Lancaster, whether a king or a queen. A government minister, the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, answers for the estate in Parliament.

The Duchy of Cornwall is older. Edward III created it in 1337 for his eldest son, Edward, the Black Prince. It passes to the monarch's eldest son when he is heir to the throne. Charles held it from 1952 until his accession. It then passed to Prince William.

Most of the Duchy of Cornwall's land lies in southwest England, including large parts of Dartmoor. It also owns property in Kennington, in south London. Under Charles, the duchy built Poundbury, an urban extension of Dorchester in Dorset.

The Crown Estate is a separate matter. It belongs to the monarch by virtue of the office, not as private property. Its revenue goes to the Treasury. A share of its profits funds the Sovereign Grant, which pays for the monarch's official duties. The Sovereign Grant Act 2011 replaced the older Civil List system with this arrangement.

Some royal property is personal. Sandringham in Norfolk and Balmoral in Scotland are privately owned by the monarch and pass by inheritance. Prince Albert bought Balmoral in 1852. Sandringham was bought in 1862 for the future Edward VII.

The monarch has paid income tax voluntarily since 1993, including on income from the Duchy of Lancaster. Charles's total personal fortune has not been publicly disclosed.

Prince Albert II has reigned over Monaco since 2005 and heads the House of Grimaldi, one of Europe's oldest ruling dynasties. The family's assets are not publicly itemized, and no verified breakdown of its holdings is available.

Albert became sovereign prince in 2005 after the death of his father, Prince Rainier III. Rainier had been on the throne since 1949. The handover was the principality's first change of ruler in more than half a century.

Rainier married the American actress Grace Kelly in 1956. Albert, born in 1958, is their only son.

The Grimaldi claim to Monaco dates to 1297. That year, François Grimaldi seized the fortress on the Rock, the outcrop that still holds the princely palace. The family has ruled the territory for most of the centuries since.

Monaco sits on the Mediterranean coast and is bordered on land by France. It is the world's second-smallest independent state, after Vatican City. Monaco is not a member of the European Union, but it uses the euro under an agreement with the EU.

The principality levies no personal income tax on most residents. French nationals living there are an exception. They are taxed by France under a 1963 agreement between the two countries.

The Monégasque state holds a majority stake in Société des Bains de Mer, the company founded in 1863 that runs the Monte-Carlo Casino. That stake belongs to the government, not to the Grimaldi family as private owners.

The prince's role is not purely ceremonial. Under Monaco's 1962 constitution, the sovereign holds executive authority. He also shares legislative power with the National Council, the principality's elected parliament.

In 2006, Albert set up the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation, which funds environmental projects.

The line of succession runs through Albert's children. He married Charlene Wittstock in 2011. Their son, Hereditary Prince Jacques, was born in 2014 alongside his twin sister, Princess Gabriella. Male-preference succession places Jacques first in line to the throne.
