#5442. Data centers are learning to be flexible

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Data centers are driving up electricity demand, but flexible power use could ease grid congestion and speed up connections

Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s AI & Tech newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest AI & tech news, analysis and insights straight to your inbox.

Picture a soccer club that bought a passenger van for its tournaments a few times a year. The van sits in a driveway the rest of the year. Buying it was the right call, because a van that wasn’t there on tournament weekend would have stranded the team.

The American power grid works the same way, and now we have numbers to show just how little of it gets used. This month, under a new state law, Virginia’s utilities reported theirs. Over the year ending in July, the distribution grid run by Dominion $D Energy, the utility behind the northern Virginia data center boom, was being used at 41% of its capacity on average.

Even in its busiest hours, the system averaged 80%, with some pockets running higher and others lower. In the state’s rural southwest, where demand has been falling, Appalachian Power reported 14% for the year and 54% at peak.

Grids are sized for the few hours a year when everyone runs the air conditioner at once, and building for those few hours is expensive. A data center that pulls full power around the clock raises that peak, and raising the peak means buying another van that mostly sits in the driveway, costing money while it gathers dust.

Researchers argued there might be a cheaper route than building, and it required something we prize in people: Flexibility. Duke $DUK researchers calculated that the existing grid could absorb nearly 100 gigawatts of new demand if the newcomers agreed to cut back its power use for roughly half a percent of the year.

The study caused a stir in energy circles, and Google $GOOGL hired its lead author. The idea came down to a trade. A customer accepts being throttled in the few hours when the local grid is stretched, and in return connects in months instead of years.

The clearest track record of this working belongs to California’s PG&E. EV charging companies, which draw heavily on the grid, saw the wait for power fall to four to eight months from one to three years before its Flex Connect pilot.

In the pilot’s first two years, the power participants asked for was there nine hours out of ten. In the hours it wasn’t, the limits cut into operations less than 1% of the time.

Batteries offered another way to ease the pressure at peak. In 2025, a data center company in Oregon secured a faster hookup from Portland General Electric $GE by agreeing to add a 31-megawatt battery, enough to run about 25,000 homes for two hours, that it could switch to if needed.

Others flexed the computing itself. Google started by putting off work that could wait whenever grids in Belgium and Taiwan ran tight. In 2024, it dialed back machine learning jobs three times when the grid around Omaha was under strain. This year it promised five utilities it would hold back as much as a gigawatt of data center demand when the grid was stretched.

Startups are selling software that slow, pause or relocate AI jobs when the grid is tight. There were plenty of ways to do it, and more kept coming.

Flexibility is already becoming required in some regions. A 2025 Texas law requires new large data centers to install equipment that lets the grid operator cut their power remotely in emergencies. Late last year, FERC, the federal agency that regulates the grid, directed the operator PJM to create interruptible transmission options for data centers built next to power plants. The Southwest Power Pool, which runs the grid across much of the Great Plains, made a similar move.

Of course, waiting is expensive, and data center queues in popular markets can run for years. Take an Nvidia $NVDA chip that costs $30,000 and is depreciated over three to five years, or $6,000 to $10,000 a year. Picture 100,000 of them in one cluster, waiting for power the way Microsoft $MSFT’s chief executive, Satya Nadella, said some of his company’s chips were last year. A year of waiting represents $600 million to $1 billion in potential computing value that goes unused.

The trade cost something on the other side too, although it was much less. For companies racing each other to build more powerful AI, even a few curtailed hours counted. If those 100,000 chips sat idle for the equivalent of 44 hours a year, the lost computing time would be worth $3 million to $5 million.

Flexibility will not fully replace the building the aging grid needs, because old equipment has to go regardless. But utilities planned to spend at least $1.4 trillion through 2030, with data centers and load growth among their top reasons, and a large transformer could take more than two years to arrive. Flexibility could shrink that bill, and that wait.

#5441. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

#5440. States agreed to ‘fully, finally, and forever’ release Meta from claims they didn’t know existed — with $459 million for Cambridge Analytica claims

I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare. My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistelblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations. I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely.

My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data.

The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse.

The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.”

The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data.

At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E.U., not events in the U.S.

A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “People You May Know,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse. Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated.

In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states.

The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.

A decade-old matter – Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal – was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.

Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “Facebook’s unjust enrichment.” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.

The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.

If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win.

Emma L. Briant, Visiting Associate Professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data and Society, University of Notre Dame

#5439. Opinion: San Francisco is delivering, while Seattle is still deliberating

by Joe Nguyễn on Nov 3, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 3, 2026 at 9:47 am

Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email [email protected].

How can a region care so much, spend billions in tax dollars and yet leave people losing faith in its future?

In Seattle, that question has become painfully familiar. People see suffering and disorder on their streets with little reason to believe help is coming. Business owners wonder whether the city values their presence or understands what it takes to keep their doors open. Even people who love this place are beginning to speak about its problems as permanent.

That growing resignation took us to San Francisco. We wanted to understand how a city so many had written off was giving people reasons to believe in its future again.

I expected to come home impressed with San Francisco. Instead, I came home with a deeper appreciation for Seattle. And an anger I am still trying to reconcile.

Seeing San Francisco make progress reminded me that Seattle has the talent and resources to do the same, perhaps even better. That is what made me frustrated. We should not have to accept people suffering on our streets and businesses struggling to stay open as conditions beyond our ability to change.

Not long ago, San Francisco had become a warning about what happens when a prosperous city loses its way. Less than two years into Mayor Daniel Lurie’s administration, that story has begun to change. Reported crime fell 22 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. According to Kidder Mathews, office vacancy declined to 26 percent in the third quarter from 31 percent in the prior year.

San Francisco still has profound problems, and the suffering we saw on its streets cannot be erased by encouraging statistics. But the people we met shared a confidence that their work could change the city’s direction. They understood what they were working toward and could explain what would happen next. Their optimism comes from seeing progress and believing they can build on it.

And I kept wondering why that felt so refreshing.

Seattle has extraordinary talent and resources, with public servants who care deeply and service providers doing demanding work under difficult conditions. Our business community helps shape the world. With that much ability and commitment here, we should feel confident that we can make our own neighborhoods safer and more welcoming.

Yet we often seem more resigned to our limitations than confident in our possibilities.

I recognize that habit because I have worked inside it. As a legislator and state agency director, I saw good intentions fall short when leaders avoided hard decisions and failed to hold people accountable for results. Even small obstacles became accepted excuses when no one took responsibility for overcoming them.

Throughout the trip, I kept looking for a more complicated explanation for the difference between San Francisco and Seattle. Eventually, the answer became impossible to miss.

Leaders expected the institutions they led to deliver results and took responsibility for making that happen. The unsettling part was how unfamiliar something so basic had come to feel.

San Francisco offered examples of what happens when leaders refuse to accept failure.

“Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.”

One example was Mayor Lurie’s response to open-air drug markets. The previous administration had already brought police, public health officials and other agencies together, but people we met described meetings that produced more updates than action. Lurie took that existing structure and gave it a clear purpose. Participants were expected to make decisions and take responsibility for carrying them out, then return with evidence of what had changed on the streets.

This approach helped illuminate a problem that is also familiar to Seattle. Officers encountering someone dangerously intoxicated often have no appropriate place to take them. Leaving the person on the street puts them and others at risk, while taking them to jail does little to address their need for care and would remove scarce law enforcement officials from patrol for hours.

San Francisco opened the RESET Center to fill this gap. Eligible individuals are able to receive brief medical supervision and stabilization, followed by connections to services. The center opened within ten months of the decision to proceed. It is a limited response to a larger crisis, but it gives people an option they lacked.

Across our conversations, leadership meant staying with a problem until the next step became possible. That requires something more uncomfortable than calling for accountability. It requires accepting that evidence may challenge an approach we have previously defended.

If we believe Seattle is a progressive city, we should ask whether our policies deliver the progress we promise. That means questioning our assumptions and changing programs when results fall short. Reconsidering an approach can feel like abandoning our values, but those values should compel us to change when people are still in need of help.

The business community must reconsider its own habits too. We often avoid politics even as public decisions shape our future. In San Francisco, business leaders helped set the agenda and backed leaders willing to act. If we want better outcomes here, we must help shape the decisions that produce them.

Government, in turn, must make clear that businesses belong here. A shop owner asking for a safe doorway and a person in crisis outside that door both deserve a response. A capable city should be able to care for both.

People form their judgment of a city through these encounters. They notice whether someone answers. They notice whether anything changes.

Over time, those experiences become confidence or despair.

San Francisco reminded me that resignation can lift. People can begin expecting more when they see reasons to believe their efforts matter.

Seattle has so much worth believing in. What we need is leadership willing to turn that promise into something people can feel.

Perhaps the most consequential thing we have lost is the expectation that we can do better.

What might we accomplish if we recovered it?

#5438. How ElevenLabs’ CTO is rolling out AI agents—and why he thinks bigger efficiency gains are ahead for the voice AI startup

Alex Holt, the field chief technology officer at ElevenLabs, is about as bullish on AI agents as a C-suite leader can get.

The AI voice startup has deployed an inbound sales development representative (SDR) agent that has handled over 3,000 customer leads this year, qualifying over 90% of those potential clients in 32 different languages without any human intervention. Yet another AI agent serves as a coach to help new sales team members role-play customers interactions, resulting in faster onboarding for that part of the workforce. There’s also a recruiting agent that conducts first-round interviews with new job candidates, and within the company’s Slack, various agents are quick to jump in and answer any employee questions about internal processes.

“I think what’s most exciting about this space is that you know you always feel like you’re on the tip of the iceberg,” says Holt. He says that the efficiency gains ElevenLabs reaps from agentic AI may feel cutting edge today, but “in six months time, you can see even more gains.”

Increasingly, CTOs and chief information officers have homed in on agentic AI as a central focus for the value they expect to extract from their frothy investments in the technology. Agentic’s share of AI value grew from 17% in 2025 to 22% this year, according to research published by consulting giant BCG, and is projected to reach 39% by 2030. And yet, most surveys find that businesses are ill-prepared to rethink workflows and orchestrate multi-agent processes, in which one agent autonomously passes along work to another.

Holt says most employees at ElevenLabs work collaboratively with agents and a majority have even built their own agents to help handle repetitive tasks. The company’s core business objectives don’t change with AI: sales teams are expected to use AI to generate more revenue at a faster pace; for customer service, satisfaction scores are closely monitored.

“It’s exactly the same business metrics,” says Holt. “This has to be an initiative that the business units themselves are driving and pushing. The agents and tech are a tool that they can leverage to do that.”

Organizationally, ElevenLabs has deployed an engineer to sit on every team across the business, and every group has fewer than 10 people. Within recruiting, for example, two forward deployed engineers work in a pod with HR colleagues with the sole objective of reducing the time it takes to get candidates through the interview process.

Today, almost all prospective candidates are initially screened by an AI recruiter when applying for a role at ElevenLabs. “That’s 30 minutes that the recruiter can spend at the end of the process, convincing you to join,” says Holt.

Holt joined ElevenLabs in September 2023 as an engineer after spending five years at software and data analytics company Palantir Technologies. He was elevated to the field CTO role in June 2026. Three months later, the startup announced that it doubled its valuation to $22 billion. CEO Mati Staniszewski recently indicated that ElevenLabs may begin to plan for an initial public offering in 2028.

The next frontier for agentic AI, says Holt, is to put more effort into multi-agent systems, enabling greater shared context and more complex work handoffs between multiple agents.

This is already under development for the company’s sales leads. The SDR agent uses voice AI to determine the seriousness of a prospective buyer, looping in a human representative after that screening process. But recently, one ElevenLabs customer was able to close a sale entirely through an interaction with two agents. First, the inbound request was fielded by the SDR agent, and later an account executive agent handled the legal documents and contracts.

“The value of that is you can now automate that whole chain for customers where it’s the simple, most repetitive mechanical cases,” says Holt. He says employees can dedicate more time to more complex inbound requests or upselling.

Holt says embracing agentic AI at this magnitude does require some patience. Is the recruiting agent helping to hire the right people? Are ElevenLabs’ customer service scores improving with AI? “Some of these metrics can take a long time,” says Holt. “We lean on the business owners to identify those leading indicators and the metrics we should be measuring.”

There are also instances where AI can act in unintended ways, an issue that’s raised alarm following recent high-profile instances in which OpenAI and Anthropic agents went rogue.

ElevenLabs says it has created a human-led monitoring and observation layer to govern its agents. But mistakes can still slip through. One customer service agent erroneously gave a small refund under $30 to a customer and failed to escalate the issue to an employee. ElevenLabs created a test case that simulated the call and the exact chain of thought and reasoning that led the agent astray, then updated the prompts and guardrails.

Holt says tracking every decision that an agent makes in this manner can actually be helpful. If a human made the same mistake, the company likely wouldn’t have noticed.

“It’s not just automating processes; it allows you to collect more data,” says Holt of agentic AI. “I expect over the next few years, the trend that we’re going to start seeing is people talking much more about optimizing these processes.”

Apple, Palantir, AMD report solid earnings after a brutal week for tech. Last week, investors put pressure on tech stocks, including those of Meta Platforms, Amazon, and especially Alphabet—whose stock had its worst day ever on Thursday—due to concerns about how much those industry titans are spending on AI infrastructure. This week, however, the tech industry has fared somewhat better as Apple set a new sales record in China Palantir reported its highest-ever revenue growth of 96%, and chipmaker AMD forecast stronger-than-expected fourth-quarter sales. Tech shares rallied even more on Wednesday, following the Democrats retaking the House and Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.

OpenAI’s latest funding round is sputtering. The ChatGPT maker has cut the target of its latest funding round and is seeking a lower valuation of $1.25 trillion, below the $1.4 trillion value it was aiming for just last month, as last week's tech sell-off in the public markets reportedly dampened interest from some large investors. The Financial Times reports that OpenAI’s funding target has been cut by $10 billion to $20 billion, while the Wall Street Journal says it has secured roughly $11 billion in commitments thus far with the deadline for this funding round set for Friday. OpenAI’s sales have fallen behind rival Anthropic, though WSJ notes that third-party data shows the former was able to capture more market share recently after cutting prices for some of its AI models.

Anthropic’s third-quarter growth slows. An amended IPO prospectus filed by Anthropic this week showed that the Claude maker generated $17 billion in revenue for the third quarter, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $1.4 billion a year earlier. But, as Fortune reports, the company’s growth rate is cooling: third-quarter revenue grew 47% sequentially, down from the revenue increase of about 144% in the second quarter from the prior three months. WSJ reports that investors are also warning Anthropic to expect a lower valuation, again citing the recent tech sell-off as a factor. Citing people familiar with the matter, Anthropic’s IPO valuation reportedly may settle closer to $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, below the $2 trillion figure that had been floated just a few months ago.

And yet, the AI boom led Marvell to announce a blockbuster deal for Lumentum. While worries about the AI boom percolate across markets, AI chip maker Marvell remains especially bullish, agreeing to pay $80 billion in an all-stock merger with optical components maker Lumentum, a deal valued at about $115 billion when including debt. Marvell says the deal will allow the combined company to address a market worth $550 billion, with Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy saying, “AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation.”

Goldman Sachs bans some AI tools. Bloomberg reports that the New York-based bank has banned most staff—excluding engineers—from using Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub, due to productivity and risk management concerns. This follows a move by CIOs and CTOs to put more controls on the AI tools that they authorize their teams to use, though these restrictions have often been attributed to rising costs, as AI bills for enterprises have increased sharply in 2026. As in the case with Goldman Sachs, engineers frequently are given more leeway, along with research and development teams.

As few jobs have been extensively redesigned around AI, CIOs play a key role in accelerating transformation. A recent survey conducted by consulting firm Deloitte featured plenty of encouraging signs regarding enterprise adoption of AI: 81% of senior leaders report AI has improved the speed of decision-making and execution; 28% see revenue gains from AI, up from 20% in the January report; and 60% say they’ve redesigned roles around AI capabilities to at least a moderate degree.

But the human component remains a conundrum. Only 15% say they’ve redesigned roles at least "extensively" around AI, a share that’s unchanged since January.

Jim Rowan, Deloitte’s US Head of AI, tells Fortune there’s a sense that even though the quality of AI tools has improved and there’s been a multi-year effort underway to transform workflows, the biggest transformation still feels “a couple of years away.” He adds that when CIOs work closely with other C-suite leaders to determine the right AI use cases to pursue, provide input on the architecture, and assess the costs, that’s when more meaningful results can be realized.

As an example of a CIO collaborating with a chief marketing officer, Rowan says, “if you can get that shared accountability to say, ‘we’re expecting this share of voice increase, a click-through rate and improvement in our marketing ads and spend here; and a reduction of third-party spend over here,’ I think that’s the handshake between the CMO-CIO and they can execute against that.” He adds that if those decisions are made lower in the leadership structure, “you lose that enterprise view and commitment.”

#5437. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5435. How ‘Entrepreneur Elevator Pitch’ Turned a 60-Second Idea Into Broadcast TV Gold

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As ‘Entrepreneur Elevator Pitch” airs nationwide, its producer shares what he’s learned watching founders vie for life-changing investment.

This fall, our investment show, Entrepreneur Elevator Pitch, airs on more than 30 TV stations (ABC, CBS, FOX, CW) across the country — and it’s an accomplishment 10 years in the making. Started as a web series in 2016, this show is not only a testament to the startup mindset, but it is a sign that people love and are moved by stories of innovation, creativity, and tenacity. Over the past six seasons I’ve produced the show, I’ve been blown away by the energy and passion I’ve witnessed from both our contestants and our audience.

For those who don’t know the premise of the show, three angel investors sit on the top floor of a building where founders have just 60 seconds to pitch in an elevator on their way up. They have to state their mission, traction, revenues, and their ask before the clock runs out.

If they’re not able to win over the investors in those 60 seconds or if they totally freak out (which happens from time to time), the founder gets sent back down to the ground floor empty-handed.

But if the founder nails the pitch, the elevator doors open and they step into the boardroom to try to seal a deal. There are rapid-fire questions, financial rundowns and demos of products ranging from snacks to apps to hardware to category-defying ideas. If the entrepreneurs are able to dazzle the investors, negotiations and bidding wars begin, with offers ranging from $25,000 to $1 million flying around the room.

Over the past 10 years, Elevator Pitch has seen some of its winning companies soar, like Trexity (which grew from $1.6 million to $14 million), Amalfi Jets (which grew to 4 million overall social followers), and Autopilot (now valued over $1 billion).

I’ve been working in television for 15 years, and producing a show like this, getting it on broadcast TV, and helping founders realize their dreams has been one of the great privileges of my life. I hope that you will check your local listings and find our show. For entrepreneurs, it is a graduate class in pitching — find out what works and doesn’t work in the boardroom.

But don’t just take it from me — in the six weeks Elevator Pitch has been on the air, we have raced past the viewership ratings of lead-in programming in top markets like Los Angeles, New York, Chicago, Dallas and Philadelphia.

If you’re an entrepreneur, I hope watching will inspire you to put your pitch together and take a chance at completely changing the trajectory of your business. Apply to be on the new season here.

#5434. Democrat wins will slow data center construction and force tech to the negotiating table after even Republican stronghold of Texas flips

The blue tidal wave that shook up U.S. politics last night ushered in several anti-data center governors in key states that could complicate Big Tech’s plans to build out the infrastructure powering AI.

Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress as a result of the midterm election Tuesday, flipping at least seven Senate seats in a historic wave that The Washington Post called a rebuke on a scale not seen since 1974. Democrats also flipped more than two dozen Republican-held House seats, with some races still undecided.

Democrats’ victories were fueled by concerns over affordability and the Iran war, as well as President Trump’s unpopularity. Yet another factor also played a role: voters’ widespread concern over the rapid buildout of data centers across the country.

Among the Democratic victories, the elections of three governors who campaigned on restricting data center development, Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Amy Acton in Ohio, and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia could be consequential for the AI industry’s future expansion.

While members of Congress would need to pass legislation, and potentially overcome a veto by President Trump, to impose new restrictions on data centers, the incoming Democratic governors have more tools at their disposal, including the power to influence permitting, regulation, and tax incentives at the state level, although some actions may require the approval of state legislatures.

We have already seen Gov. Abbott wield the power of the governor’s office to take action on data centers in Texas, the state with more data center capacity operating and under construction than any other, according to Baxtel, and which is projected to hold nearly 30% of U.S. data center capacity by 2028, according to a Bloom Energy report.

Abbott, who was defeated Tuesday by Governor-elect Hinojosa, initially supported data centers, yet he adjusted his stance earlier this year amid widespread concerns over their resource use. In June, Abbott directed state regulators to develop measures requiring data centers to cover the costs for the energy infrastructure they use for their operations. In August, he halted new grid connection approvals for data centers while regulators conducted an audit of proposed projects. And later directed state officials to enforce water-use reporting requirements and instructed regulators to pause new data center permits until audits on their electricity and water use were completed.

Hinojosa, for her part, said Gov. Abbott’s tough talk on data centers was “nothing more than an election year stunt.” Hinojosa promised in the run up to the election that, were she to win, she would impose a moratorium on data center construction and eliminate subsidies and tax breaks awarded to major data center developers.

Governor-elect Amy Acton in Ohio made similar promises, calling for a conditional moratorium on new data centers unless developers agree to cover all their utility costs, use union labor, and meet environmental standards. Meanwhile, in Georgia, Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms also promised a temporary statewide pause on new data center construction to assess the industry’s impact on electricity bills, communities, and the environment.

Across eight major North American markets, a record 7,481 megawatts of data center capacity was under construction during the first half of 2026, a nearly 25% increase from a year earlier, according to commercial real estate firm CBRE.

And yet, taken together, the election of these three governors represents a “new reality” for tech companies that have been pouring billions of dollars into data center construction and will now need to reassess, said longtime tech analyst Dan Ives, of merchant banking firm Yorkville Ives.

While Trump may veto any draconian AI safety or regulatory laws passed by a Democratic-controlled Congress. The newfound influence of AI skeptical politicians in Congress will force tech companies to come to the negotiating table to reach compromises on AI-related legislation, Ives wrote in a Wednesday note.

“Tech needs to adjust and focus on a slower pace of this AI rollout,” he said in an email.

Shares of companies involved with the AI compute and data center construction fell Wednesday including CoreWeave, Applied Digital, and Cipher Digital. Yet, the overall market was up as of afternoon trading, with the S&P 500 up 1.82% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 1.94%.

Ives said in the note Wednesday that while tech companies may now face obstacles to building out their data center capacity, the Democratic wins could actually be a positive for tech stocks as it will likely force hyperscalers, like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, to slow down their capital expenditures, which are expected to hit at most $828 billion in 2026.

“The Street still is way underestimating the future revenue growth and profitability that AI will bring to the tech world (and other industries) over the next few years,” he wrote. “Now it will happen at a more measured pace which is likely a good thing in the eyes of many investors…and the market will digest this news and move forward.”

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5432. Companies Are Paying Up to $1.45 Million for This In-Demand Job

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Demand for a specialized engineering role is driving impressive paychecks as companies compete for talent.

A highly sought-after engineering job is commanding a hefty price as employers compete to fill positions.

According to a recent Wall Street Journal report, demand for one specialized engineering role is pushing compensation into seven-figure territory. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) put agentic AI into production. They adapt AI tools to a company’s operations and help get those tools running.

Companies are increasingly bringing FDEs onto their own payrolls rather than relying on outside firms to make AI technology work, Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of recruiting firm Christian & Timbers, said in a new interview with the Journal.

Christian said top-notch FDEs are making between $586,000 and $1.45 million a year in total pay, with equity and bonuses comprising 52% to 66% of total pay.

Demand for FDE services has swelled as businesses discover they need hands-on support to put AI into practice. The engineers typically work for technology companies like Palantir or OpenAI, or consulting firms such as Accenture and McKinsey. However, Christian said other businesses are now hiring FDEs directly to develop AI applications internally.

The move to hire shifts the FDE job from a temporary one to a permanent responsibility. FDEs are now specialized in building reliable AI systems for a single employer and ensuring that the spending yields a financial return.

“Every company is thinking, ‘We got to do this ourselves,’” Christian said.

He added that hiring FDEs internally also allows businesses to keep their data private instead of sharing it with engineers supplied by outside vendors.

Recent job postings from Target, Barclays, Bausch and Lomb and American Express point to growing interest in hiring FDEs, per the Journal. The companies want engineers who can translate loosely defined objectives into working AI agent systems and expand experimental projects into tools used across their businesses.

Competition for these engineers is fierce, with corporate employers, technology companies and consulting firms all pursuing the same limited talent pool. Christian & Timbers estimates that the U.S. has about 17,000 FDEs, only around 2,000 of whom qualify as top-tier specialists.

At cloud-based data platform Snowflake, chief revenue officer Jonathan Beaulier told the Journal that recruiting FDEs was particularly difficult. The company’s frontier engineering group works directly with customers to develop AI applications. To help staff that team, the company is drawing on employees from other divisions, he said.

Growing demand for FDEs has helped create businesses such as Distyl AI, founded by former Palantir employees Arjun Prakash and Derek Ho. The startup places engineers inside client companies to help shape their AI plans and build the tools to carry them out.

“The most common question being asked by the CEO of a Fortune 500 today is not, ‘How do I deploy AI?’ It’s actually, ‘What should my business model be?’” Prakash said in an interview with the Journal. “That partnership requires a certain flavor of forward-deployed engineering with a heavier strategy muscle.”

#5431. ‘He basically gets to steer a political party’: Elon Musk is $474 million poorer post-election, but it may not have deterred his influence on 2028

Elon Musk’s nearly half-a-billion dollar bet on Republican midterm victories is a day late and many dollars short, but whether the world’s richest person’s political investments were all for nought remains to be seen.

The tech billionaire donated at least $474 million to Republican candidates ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, nearly twice what he donated ahead of the 2024 presidential election. That sum included around $200 million to election efforts in Texas alone.

Yet Musk had little to show for it: Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott were both trounced by Democratic opponents. Shares of SpaceX and Tesla, which are both headquartered in Texas, were down on Wednesday following the news.

Musks’s other donations included $30 million the the Congressional Leadership Fund, the primary super PAC back of House Republicans, as well as $44 million to other Republicans groups and candidates working to elect federal officials. He joined a16z’s Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz ($116.4 million) and OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman and his wife Anna ($50 million) as the party’s biggest donors for the midterms.

The shock of the hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending without the intended results was a clear example of the risks associated with political donations.

“I think this might just be the biggest defeat for big money in politics in American history,” Logan Phillips, founder of the election forecasting site Race to the White House, told Fortune.

Musk is certainly acquainted with this risk—and while he may not have seen the election outcomes he poured unprecedented amounts of money into, the jury is still out on if he has lost the good and influence of key Republicans, or if he’s laying the groundwork for the 2028 election, campaign finance experts argued.

Musk did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

While the results of the election prove money isn’t the make-or-break factor in electing candidates, Virginia Commonwealth University political science professor Alex Keena argues it’s better wielded in the context of setting the table for future political fights.

“Those of us who study campaign money have been sort of realizing this for the past decade: It’s not about helping someone win,” Keena told Fortune. “That messaging domination, it’s just not going to happen with money. Instead…first and foremost, money is affecting what we’re talking about.”

Political donations rather serve the primary purpose of dictating the topics a party publicly discusses or pursues, such as climate change, data centers, or economic reform. By that standard, Musk could very much still have influence on the future of the Republican party.

The magnitude of Musk’s donations also indicate a level of commitment to President Donald Trump, who could prove to be an ally to him as he races against time to complete a SpaceX-Tesla merger that Democrats have signalled to heavily scrutinize.

“He basically gets to steer a political party,” Keena said. “This is one of the biggest influences of money. It’s not just about who wins. It’s about setting the agenda and what types of issues we talk about.”

That agenda may only take Musk so far. While Trump has threatened to “veto everything” a Democratic majority in the House and Senate pass, Democrats can leverage subpoena powers, which don’t require the president’s signature. Officials will want to investigate Musk’s public companies and his role in the federal government, which included the Department of Government Efficiency gaining illegal access to sensitive data while failing to achieve one of its goals of decreasing the federal deficit.

“We definitely have a lot of questions about Elon Musk’s role in DOGE and it is something we plan to investigate,” Sara Guerrero, a spokesperson for top Oversight Committee Democrat Rep. Robert Garcia of California, said last month.

Musk’s very public and very impactful role in the federal government may be one reason why his campaign efforts fell short, according to Casey Michel, author of United States of Oligarchy: How America’s Wealthiest Ally with Dictators, Weaken the U.S., and Destroy Democracy.

Michel told Fortune that Musk’s DOGE was effectively a fourth branch of government that could leverage its political powers for private sector gain. A Washington Post analysis published last month found two dozen former DOGE staffers leveraged government connections to enter the private sector and backed or founded startups that raised more than $500 million in venture capital and funding. Following Musk’s official departure of DOGE in May 2025, his companies minted an estimated $10 billion in government contracts, led by SpaceX.

The public flaunting of power could have soured Republican voters on Musk, or at least lessened his political influence, Michel argued.

“I’m struggling to think of a clearer example of what happens to an oligarch when they place themselves front and center in a political system like we saw with Musk over the last two years,” he said. “This was always the risk that he was running in injecting himself, quite literally, into the White House, as well as dominating the financial or campaign donation landscape, and in a certain sense, it’s not surprising to see this kind of blowback generated.

“This makes clear at the end of the day that Musk’s financing is no longer the asset that it once was in 2024,” Michel added, “but is now a very clear liability both to those who are receiving it, like the Ken Paxtons of the world, but also to himself.”

There’s reason to believe that regardless if Musk’s political stock has gone up or down, he could still be a major donor in future elections.

“This is like him deciding to go get Starbucks on the way home from work,” Keena said.

There’s some truth behind the sentiment. Jennifer Heerwig, a political sociology professor at SUNY Stony Brook University, said one significant predictor for someone making a political contribution is their income.

“Assuming that he remains the world’s richest man, I wouldn’t find it shocking to see him again entering politics and making huge donations to super PACs,” she told Fortune. “Whether or not he’ll do it at the same scale, I think, remains to be seen.”

Musk has appeared to change his mind on political donations in the past. In May 2025, he said he could cut back on political spending, clarifying he would donate if he saw a reason, but that he currently saw no reason.

“I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” Musk said in an interview with Bloomberg at the Qatar Economic Forum at the time. “I think I’ve done enough.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5430. Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5429. This Ultra-Luxury Concierge Firm Costs $150,000 Just to Join. One Client Spent $24 Million on a Birthday.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s a problem most of us would love to have. What if you had so much money that you needed to hire someone just to help you enjoy it?

For about 145 families, that someone is Fischer Unlimited, a New York luxury concierge firm that charges $150,000 just to become a client, plus a $25k annual fee. “Their time is precious,” says CEO and president Stacy Fischer-Rosenthal. “They really want to make sure that professionals are handling their needs.”

Take Taylor Swift tickets. During the Eras Tour, one client wanted to go at the last minute. Fischer didn’t just find seats. Stacy’s son, Max Rosenthal, the company’s vice president, says the firm got the client into the owner’s box and arranged a private helicopter transfer for the weekend.

What’s their secret? “It’s about the relationships,” Max says. The trick is finding the right person to call, then having that person persuade whoever has what your client wants.

Getting people past the velvet rope is the family business. Stacy’s father, Bill Fischer, founded the company as Fischer Travel more than 60 years ago. He started charging fees once he figured out how to get clients into places like the Hotel du Cap in Antibes, which didn’t work with travel agents. About 30 years ago, he asked every client to pay $5,000 to stay on. Some left, some stayed, and the firm went all in on high-end travelers.

Stacy joined 44 years ago, when her clients were twentysomething hedge funders who wanted to skip the line at nightclubs. Now she handles everything from dinner reservations to birthday gifts, which is why the company recently changed its name. “We really do so much more than travel,” she says. Her staff of about 45 includes no independent contractors, and some families have been clients for three generations.

And the requests can get huge. Last August, in a scene straight out of Succession, a client chartered Belmond’s Royal Scotsman train for a weeklong birthday trip with 20 friends. The firm paid four booked parties to travel a different week. At a pop-up shop at Gleneagles, guests were fitted for tartans and Barbour jackets, with everyone’s sizes already stocked. The client brought 70 pieces of luggage, so valets ran outfits to each cabin from trailers full of clothes. There were vintage cars, castle tours with a Scottish lord and a fireworks finale in Edinburgh with 100 more guests. About 400 people worked on it. The bill is coming in around $24 million.

Other jobs require detective work. One client noticed that Prince Harry always wears a bracelet he was given in Africa after his mother died, and he wanted a replica. Stacy’s vendor in South Africa couldn’t pin down where it came from. Then a business partner offered to ask Meghan Markle. Harry’s former nanny, who had been on that trip, helped trace the bracelet to the village where it was made. The all-in price was about $15,000, including a book documenting the search.

Max insists the firm doesn’t just throw money at problems. “No very successful person became very rich by spending recklessly,” he says. But white-glove service doesn’t come cheap. “We’re not a discount shop,” Max says. “But if you want access, if you want to be able to walk into a hotel and not check into a front desk and just go straight to the room, that’s the service that we provide.”

Here’s a problem most of us would love to have. What if you had so much money that you needed to hire someone just to help you enjoy it?

For about 145 families, that someone is Fischer Unlimited, a New York luxury concierge firm that charges $150,000 just to become a client, plus a $25k annual fee. “Their time is precious,” says CEO and president Stacy Fischer-Rosenthal. “They really want to make sure that professionals are handling their needs.”

Take Taylor Swift tickets. During the Eras Tour, one client wanted to go at the last minute. Fischer didn’t just find seats. Stacy’s son, Max Rosenthal, the company’s vice president, says the firm got the client into the owner’s box and arranged a private helicopter transfer for the weekend.
