#5427. ‘The best thing that you can do for your career is to make yourself redundant’: Inside Stellantis’ AI push after the ‘starting gun went off’

The Grand Cherokee is lined with wood paneling, its windshield is cracked, and chunks are cut out of its side-view mirrors like pierced ears. That’s where the cameras go, a grinning Joydip Saha tells me from behind the wheel. The manager of Stellantis’ hands-free driving project lovingly taps what he calls “the most broken-up car,” jerry-rigged with a yellow box sitting on the dashboard that lets a human grab control. It’s an industry-standard “kill switch” used in many prototype vehicles. In technical terms, the safety driver can hit the kill switch to disconnect power to the advanced driver assist system module, stopping the ADAS system from controlling the vehicle. Then, the driver has full control over the vehicle.

Another piece of equipment connected to the kill switch — the STLA AutoDrive L2++ system embedded in the vehicle — beeps when it needs him to take control, a bit like a dog wearing a smart collar.

And it’s confused. We are in the bowels of the Chrysler Technology Center in suburban Auburn Hills, Mich., navigating through the rabbit warren of a parking structure on the campus built by Lee Iacocca, the former Fortune posterboy who broke ground on the 500-acre site in 1986 and dedicated it in 1991, at a cost the company puts at about $1 billion. With the headquarters tower added in 1996, it spans 5.4 million square feet, the second-largest building in the U.S. by floor space, behind only the Pentagon.

Stellantis still runs its North American engineering out of Iacocca’s building, and the people who work there still say “all under one roof.” Inside, it’s a pure shot of early ‘90s design. Skinny escalators climb skyward around an octagonal skylight, like a Clinton-era MC Escher drawing.

The diamond-shaped parking garage attached to it is unique and confounding. Saha’s development mule heads toward the wrong exit and Saha has to put his hands on the wheel Even he finds the garage complicated. Auburn Hills’ suburban roads are much better for a test drive and I watch Saha’s mule smoothly navigate an intersection where two Michiganders decide to both make illegal multi-lane changes within seconds of each other.

Saha, the global engineering manager who serves as the owner of Stellantis’ L2++/hands-free door-to-door supervised automated driving system, has been at this longer than most. He worked on the Chrysler Pacifica that Stellantis supplied for Waymo’s first robotaxi in Arizona, then managed a group that integrated Level 4 autonomy with partners including Aurora and Lyft. He still test-drives every new software build himself, as often as twice a week, because he considers any problem a customer faces problems  to be his responsibility. He said his team built the Cherokee’s hands-free system in six weeks with the help of AI tools, when a similar project used to take a year or even 18 months.

He has a rule for AI, though: “I will not let people use AI to architect stuff because they will forget how to debug stuff,” he said. In a safety-critical business, he adds, engineers have to be able to answer every question.

Across two days of interviews at the technology center, engineers told Fortune that AI has turned yearlong projects into weeks and overnight simulations into minutes. Stellantis wants that speed to cut development time on its new computing and cockpit software, STLA Brain and STLA SmartCockpit as part of a general push to speed vehicle development from four years to 24 months, starting with two models in 2027. But nearly everyone who described a speed-up also described checking the machine’s work. Stellantis also has problems bigger than time savings. The company has 14 brands, a European business that is losing money, and a second-quarter adjusted operating margin of 1.8%, while CEO Antonio Filosa has set a margin target of 7% for 2030.

Wall Street isn’t waiting. Stellantis is the member of Detroit’s Big Three most exposed to Europe, which accounted for about 38% of its 2025 revenue. (GM sold its European brands, Opel and Vauxhall, in 2017 to PSA, one of the companies that later merged to form Stellantis.) Europe also leans much harder toward electric vehicles than truck-happy America: : battery-electric cars made up 17.4% of new EU registrations last year, according to ACEA, compared with 7.8% of U.S. sales, according to Cox Automotive.

Stellantis had also bet heavily on EVs in North America, and it took the biggest hit in Detroit after the $7,500 federal EV tax credit ended on Sept. 30, 2025. In February, Stellantis wrote down roughly €22.2 billion (about $26.5 billion), more than Ford’s $19.5 billion charge in December or the $7.6 billion GM took across two charges. Stellantis shares fell 25% that day, and the reverberations are still being felt, with the stock down nearly 60% year-to-date.

Mel Roberts, the director of North American infotainment and features planning, who plans the displays inside Stellantis vehicles five to eight years out, said AI was not her biggest surprise of the last several years. “What I couldn’t anticipate is just the complete collapse of the electrification ambitions and how that really did affect all of our future plans,” she said. “It trickled into everything.”

Stellantis is the only one of Detroit’s Big Three to be legally headquartered abroad, in the Netherlands. It’s the result of a pandemic-era merger in 2021 between Fiat Chrysler and the PSA Group that brought iconic European brands such as Peugeot and Citroën together with Fiat, Jeep and Ram. That gives it a distinctly international air, as Fortune met executives born in France, Mexico and Bangladesh within minutes of each other, along with a Michigander back from a few years stationed in Paris.

The mergers also left behind a machine built by committee. Ben Zawodni, manager of software engineering, is working to fold the hundreds of electronic control units, each a small computer with its own job, into a central “brain” called, naturally, STLA Brain. Over the decades, he says, the car’s architecture had evolved over time to really mirror the supply chain. “We were bolting on features.”

Amanda French, who leads the company’s platform teams, is tackling the same problem one layer down. Stellantis historically built separate platforms, each to a fixed size. Its new platform, STLA One, is built to stretch from small B-segment cars to midsize D-segment vehicles. The company says it is designed to grow into a mega platform supporting 30+ models and targeting more than 2 million units by 2035. Asked whether building it felt like playing with Legos, French responded, “Yeah, with a lot more people and emotions involved.”

Upstairs at the technical center, Chief Engineering & Technology Officer Ned Curic is a self-described “intense” but talkative and warm presence. He came to Stellantis by way of Amazon, with previous stints at Microsoft and Toyota. He explained that Stellantis is not where it needs to be. Some teams show “phenomenal successes,” he said. In building that culture, he said, “as a whole organization, we are not there.”

Curic sounds exasperated with an industry that has piled on complexity. Cars now come with “five screens, like digital noise, like 350 features,” he said, and automakers have historically tended to “checklist the heck out of the features” without measuring how people actually use them. He said he learned from Toyota that “the highest quality part that you have in a car is the part that you don’t have in a car.” In Stellantis’ research on drivers, for instance, he said most people preferred a mechanical stick to a button on a screen.

At Amazon, Curic received Jeff Bezos’ notorious emails forwarding on customer complaints. The body of each email was a single question mark. “I never found it stressful,” Curic said. “Never.” One executive would handle the problem, he explained, and the others would each write a couple of paragraphs to help.

From Amazon and Toyota, Curic also brought small teams from the “two-pizza rule” and single owners for each system, so engineers who once sat in separate groups can’t blame each other when something breaks. “If you see something that’s wrong, you just pick it up,” he said. “I own it.”

The hardest idea he’s selling is that “the best thing that you can do for your career is to make yourself redundant.” He has done it himself several times by getting a team in good shape, leaving, and starting something new. For that to work, Curic said, the company has to make sure there is always a new opportunity for those people, and that leaders need maturity and confidence. Asked whether Detroit’s long run of hard times makes people defensive about change, he replied that while there is always a bit of a fear, change is a lot more accepted, ”and actually sought after.”

The man telling engineers to make themselves redundant is also hiring them. At the Paris auto show in October, Curic told Bloomberg that Stellantis would add “multiple hundreds” of engineers in Europe and the U.S. this year.

The pressure lands on engineers like Zawodni and French. Both of them are tackling Stellantis’ tricky margins issue by simplifying the wiring for each vehicle to bring the manufacturing into alignment, cutting costs and boosting Stellantis’ profits back to where they need to be. “The AIs aren’t going to tell us what the new platforms are,” Zawodni said.

Zawodni said he started working on consolidating the cars’ central computing during COVID, when engineers went fully remote and Stellantis set up labs in India, Poland and North America that could be logged into from anywhere. A proof of concept for a global observability platform, which monitors software deep inside the car’s computers, took a week. Before agentic coding tools, he remembered something like that would take six months. And defects that took two to three weeks to fix shrank to two to three days. “We knew that we had to really reimagine all of our time,” Zawodni said. Did that scare him? “How exciting, right?”

French, a cheerful engineer from southern Indiana, lit up when the conversation turned to AI, though hers was a more measured take than Zawodni’s. She said human judgment “cannot be replaced,” but AI helps her pull together requirements and bills of materials stored in regional systems that were never built to talk to each other, because Stellantis is “made up from a number of different companies.” She compared AI to an interactive form of Cliffs Notes she wished for in school.

Zawodni said his team was not all as excited about the AI breakthroughs as he was. “I think there was a starting gun, and that starting gun went off,” he said. “Some people heard it, and some people didn’t.” Of his own engineers, he calls it a mixed bag. “Engineers are really afraid of losing their core skills,” he said. They want to know why a semicolon in a coding language does what it does. He called that “a valid curiosity,” but argued that it doesn’t get Stellantis to its goals. He wants them to become architects, and eventually chief architects.

The tools haven’t lightened Zawodni’s own load. “Agentic tools, they’ve made our work so much easier,” he said. “So why am I working so much harder?” He estimates he works at least twice as hard as before. “I feel a tremendous sense of urgency.” He said, “I really hope that we can transition responsibly … especially our people.”

Anne Laliron, a French engineer who runs Stellantis’ roughly 400-person tech research group, gave up her office after COVID so her team can always find her, and she lights up talking about their energy. Her job is deciding which big bets to make. Stellantis can’t afford to do everything, so it designs battery cells in-house and partners with startups for the rest. “If you want to embrace everything,” she said, “you are at risk of spreading your effort.”

For Stellantis, partnering is a way to punch above its weight. The company brings in Wayve, a British startup, for the perception software in its hands-free driving, works with the French startup Tiamat on sodium-ion batteries, with Zeta Energy on lithium-sulfur batteries, and owns a stake in the Chinese EV maker Leapmotor, selling its cars outside of China through the joint venture Leapmotor International. Laliron said the habit runs deep at Stellantis and is less common at other automakers. Curic wants a culture where “it doesn’t have to be invented here,” and he said the learning with Leapmotor runs both ways: “We learned a lot… we also taught them a lot.” Stellantis runs batteries the same way, Laliron said: design in-house, partner with startups, and leave mass production to its gigafactory partners.

Their biggest bet sits on a stage nearby: a battery-electric Dodge Charger prototype carrying a solid-state battery from Factorial, a Massachusetts startup Stellantis has worked with since 2021. The two companies run it as one team, and Factorial co-founder Siyu Huang says the startup has done it with $250 million in capital, a fraction of what some competitors have spent. The car worked the first time they turned the key. But Huang puts the technology three to five years from automotive production, and Laliron cuts about 10% of her group’s projects every year when they don’t pan out. “It’s always painful,” she said.

Elsewhere, the speed-ups are real, but still small next to Stellantis’ problems. Arturo Guzman was among the first to bring AI into the company’s aerodynamics work, about five years ago, after a startup struggled to explain it to him in a side conversation at a conference.

Now he explains it to vice presidents, and he starts by taking the mystery out. “There’s no miracles. There’s no magic,” he said. “For us being engineers, all this is a Python code.” Run through his team’s model, a design change to a Ram pickup’s front splitter returns a drag estimate in about three minutes. The full simulation used to take 14 to 24 hours. He tells his directors it’s like an intern. His younger engineers get a different metaphor: R2-D2 from Star Wars. “You just give it a task and come back and see what it did.”

Guzman said the time his team saves goes to “other stuff.” His team now generates new guidelines, takes requests from across the company, and mines its simulation data for patents. “Now I tell them, just send me the data,” he said.

Through the doors to the wind tunnel, the giant equipment runs at pretty much the same pace it always has. It still tests “typically, one car a day,” said Steve Kubiak, a deadpan Michigander who started at Chrysler in 1992 and has supervised the tunnel for about 10 years. Asked whether the process has changed over time, he said, “No, it’s always been the same.” The analysis is speeding up even if the testing isn’t. A colleague, Todd Lounsberry, gives AI the data from the last 20 runs of a test and asks what it sees. Asked how someone becomes the manager of a wind tunnel, Kubiak responded, “First you get a wind tunnel.”

Other engineers are keeping AI on a short leash. Mohammed Malik, who runs Stellantis’ driving simulators from the Automotive Research & Development Centre in Windsor, Ontario, said his group is “keeping it in the box,” but even so, technology has transformed his work. Malik at work is like a life-size, immersive game of Mario Kart, the classic racing game where Nintendo characters pick their car and track then try to dodge obstacles to the finish line.

His job has been transformed by his simulator more than by AI. Engineers used to tune a vehicle on a computer, build a prototype and only then find out how it felt. Now a driver can feel the computer model before anything is built, and Malik can swap springs on the fly. He can test 10 tires in an hour, something no prototype can do. His team has scanned about 20 roads, from racetracks to local streets, in 10-centimeter squares, and it trades models with colleagues in Brazil and Italy instead of shipping cars across oceans.

Malik plays me a video of a full-size Stellantis body that lacks any wheels — instead it’s suspended on what appear to be mechanical spider-legs, bobbing up and down, back and forth in front of a giant TV screen with a track. Asked whether he ever played Mario Kart, he said he has a track of his own, built by a student. “You can drive the Rainbow Road if you want,” he beams from behind his bushy mustache.

AI’s role is narrower. A simulator run produces thousands of channels of data, and when a car hits a bump and “swirls a little bit,” Malik asks AI which channel to look at. His ambition is much bigger: feed an agent every test driver’s scorecards from every region, ask it “what does it take to make a Jeep,” and let it drive the simulator itself until the answer feels right. For now, he said, the company is moving at a very slow pace and wants some form of control. “Some of the stuff we want to do, we can do today,” he said. “And some of the stuff we want to do, we cannot.”

The bigger surprise has been people’s willingness, or lack thereof, to adapt. Veteran test drivers who spent 10 or 20 years in physical prototypes were slow to move to the simulator. Young engineers with racing setups in their basements took to it right away. Laliron has seen the same thing. Experienced engineers carry old failures with them, she said, and sometimes “their brain is closing doors.”

Some people have made peace with work that is better but not faster. Roberts said her AI research tool returns 10 to 15 sources, and she has to check every one. “I don’t think it saves time,” she said, though it makes her work more “robust.”

Alison Rahm, the chief vehicle engineer for midsize and large SUVs, has seen this before. She is moving back to Michigan after two years running Stellantis’ European car lineup from Paris, and she remembers a staff meeting in 1997, when her boss told the room they were getting something new called email. “All of us were in a total panic,” she said. They went back to their desks and tried it anyway.

AI now runs checks that people used to do by hand, Rahm said, like going down a list of about 1,000 engineering design practices. That frees engineers to ask whether the rules themselves are right. But she isn’t ready to stop double-checking. For years after virtual crash testing arrived, she notes, engineers still crashed real cars into the walls to convince themselves the situations were right.

Asked how long it will take to trust AI the same way, Rahm paused. “I think we need another life cycle to prove to ourselves that our assumptions were right.” While cautioning that different products have different life cycles, she deliberated. “I would say four years.” That would land in 2030, the year Filosa has promised a 7% margin.

Saha drives us back into Iacocca’s garage, and puts his hands back on the wheel of the Cherokee as the diamond-shaped parking structure looms. The robot needs a guiding hand coming home.

Saha takes a long view on when the AI game will shake out. As we roll into a smooth parking job, he turns to me and says he’s a Game of Thrones fan (his favorite character is Robb Stark). While he works in logic, he explains, he likes fantasy because he finds he needs “to be a little bit philosophical” with the other side of his brain. “Creativity is very important.”

Saha takes a long view on when the AI game will shake out. As we roll into a smooth parking job, he turns to me and says he’s a Game of Thrones fan (his favorite character is Robb Stark). While he works in logic, he explains, he likes fantasy because he finds he needs “to be a little bit philosophical” with the other side of his brain. “Creativity is very important.”

Humans have adapted and thrived to date by figuring out creative solutions, he said. “We were never the strongest animal in the world,” he said, riffing a bit in the style of Game of Thrones writer George R.R. Martin. He suggests that several hundred years of industrialization led people sometimes to get used to process-oriented thinking. “My understanding is we’re going to leave behind the process-oriented world because AI is going to help us. And my personal belief is that’s actually good.”

“There will be some loss,” Saha said, as there is with any technological shift. But he pointed out that humans have adapted to the natural world through creativity over and over again. “People are going to figure out how to tame AI, too.”

#5426. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5425. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5424. Replacing Entry-Level Talent With AI Is a Costly Mistake. Here’s What to Do Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is changing how businesses think about hiring, but eliminating junior roles can create problems that outweigh the short-term savings.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you ask a group of business leaders where AI should fit within their teams, many will give the same reply: It can take over the kind of work we used to assign to interns. This view is easy to understand. AI is good at research, summaries and first drafts, so the entry-level role starts to look optional. However, I believe that’s a mistake — and an expensive one.

Cutting junior roles may save money this year. It also removes two things AI can’t replace: those people who see your business with fresh eyes, and the pipeline that produces your future managers.

The most obvious objection is that an AI tool costs less than a salary and doesn’t require onboarding. And yes, if you only look at this year’s budget, replacing junior roles can look like a smart call.

The problem is what that decision costs later. Every senior person on your team started their career somewhere. As Lucy Beaumont, global SVP of product at SHL, told CNBC, entry-level roles are where people make their first mistakes and learn how a business really runs.

If nobody is trained today, who will be leading in 10 years? Cut that training ground, and you’re left with two options: Pay a premium to poach experienced people from competitors, or promote people who never learned the basics.

Meanwhile, graduates get stuck in a loop: Roles ask for experience, and experience requires someone to take a chance and hire them. ZipRecruiter’s 2026 graduate report found that 81.6% of grads who worked during college are now employed, compared with 40.7% of those who didn’t. So someone has to break the loop, and the companies that do get first pick of loyal, motivated talent other employers overlook.

Experienced teams run on routine, and that’s a big part of what makes them efficient. The trade-off is that familiar processes rarely get a second look, even when there’s a better way to do them.

New employees have the benefit of fresh eyes and a fresh perspective. They notice onboarding steps with unnecessary friction or features customers will never use. They then ask, “Why do we do it that way?” and sometimes this leads to new and improved processes.

Of course, I have a bias; I joined AnswerConnect in 2006 as a temp-to-hire with little experience. Early on, the founder asked how things were going and really listened when I shared feedback on pain points I had experienced. I saw almost immediate changes, and the idea that I could make a difference as a brand-new employee changed everything for me. I chose to stay, and I’ve grown throughout the organization and helped influence change along the way. This is baked into our company culture and makes us stronger.

None of this means avoiding AI. It means using it to improve junior roles, not eliminate them.

Leave the role in place and redesign it instead. Make a list of the actual activities entry-level employees carry out each week. Pass repetitive tasks to AI, and return the time gained to the kinds of work where people develop fastest, such as talking to customers, solving problems and making judgment calls.

Teach new employees to use AI critically. Teach them to check AI output, recognize when it is incorrect and know when a person should stay involved. These skills will only become more valuable, and they’re easier to develop early on than to correct later.

Don’t leave new hires to work it out alone. Build learning into the job from day one: working sessions with experienced colleagues, shared projects and paid time for training. Your senior people benefit, too. You often realize how you do something could be better when you explain it.

Encourage curiosity and feedback. Make it easy for new hires to tell you what they see:

Every business will use AI. What matters is what you do with the time and money it frees up: bank the savings and shrink the team, or invest in the people who’ll be running your company in 10 years.

People who are trained and trusted care more, and customers can tell. So which company will you be: the one that stopped developing talent, or the one that built it?

If you ask a group of business leaders where AI should fit within their teams, many will give the same reply: It can take over the kind of work we used to assign to interns. This view is easy to understand. AI is good at research, summaries and first drafts, so the entry-level role starts to look optional. However, I believe that’s a mistake — and an expensive one.

Cutting junior roles may save money this year. It also removes two things AI can’t replace: those people who see your business with fresh eyes, and the pipeline that produces your future managers.

The most obvious objection is that an AI tool costs less than a salary and doesn’t require onboarding. And yes, if you only look at this year’s budget, replacing junior roles can look like a smart call.

#5423. After the midterms, Big Tech’s AI data center problem is only getting bigger

After ChatGPT launched in late 2022, tech companies raced to open data centers at unprecedented rates, pouring billions of dollars into AI hubs in states like Texas and Ohio. Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, and others did so even as polling showed the centers were highly unpopular among a large swath of the U.S. population.

On Tuesday, the issue came to a decisive tipping point. U.S. voters delivered an overwhelming victory for Democratic candidates throughout the country that will upend the halls of power in Washington and data center hotbeds like Texas. While tech companies have established years-long plans to keep opening the centers, and are regularly plugging more online, they will be met with new state and national political leaders whose mandate is to slow down the unpopular facilities. They also now face a wave of voter rejection on numerous projects across the U.S.

Voters sided against data center development in all but one of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts tracked by Redbud Consulting, a Washington, D.C., polling and data science firm, according to preliminary results.

That includes Piqua, a 20,000-person city in west central Ohio, where Meta is planning to spend $1 billion to construct a data center with a capacity of up to 1.4 gigawatts. Residents voted to recall the mayor and two city commissioners who supported the project.

In Ohio, voters in at least 14 municipalities approved data center bans or other restrictions, showing that the opposition extended well beyond a handful of high-profile projects.

And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated longtime Republican Gov. Greg Abbott after campaigning on a moratorium on data center development until lawmakers establish additional protections for residents. Texas has more than 400 data center facilities and many more under construction, according to the American Edge Project and Technology Councils of North America.

“Most definitely, there will be challenges — two or three steps forward, one step back,” Baron Fung, senior research director at market research firm Dell’Oro Group, told Fortune, speaking about what Big Tech companies now face. “There could be delays … trying to address any kind of guidelines that weren’t really reinforced before regarding data centers.”

Fung said overall progress will continue, but companies may shift projects as they deal with pushback, and they will be asked to assume more of the financial and energy burden going forward rather than relying as much on municipalities.

Elon Musk, whose SpaceX expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditures in the quarter ending in December, wrote on X Tuesday night that “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” Musk spent more than $200 million supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who lost.

The unpopularity of data centers in the U.S. has been a central theme of the AI revolution. Most Americans oppose data centers and are more fearful about AI than hopeful, according to recent Pew Research Center polls. During the second quarter of this year, at least 45 data center projects worth roughly $68 billion were disrupted by local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs.

The hyperscalers opening the centers have themselves warned about disruptions to their plans. In September, Oracle executives noted during an earnings call that the company doesn’t assume every project will arrive on time, that it has backup options, and that it brings large campuses online in phases. The company has developments across the U.S. and internationally, so “all of our eggs are not in a single basket,” Co-CEO Clay Magouyrk said.

Oracle, in particular, has stood out for its risk-taking during the AI buildout, having more than $125 billion in debt and other notes payable and fundraising aggressively. Earlier this year, the company said it would need to raise between $45 billion and $50 billion in 2026 alone to fund its infrastructure expansion.

Before Tuesday’s election results, Microsoft, Amazon, and other major companies had mounted charm offensives in communities throughout the country in the hopes of winning over weary residents. The strategy has centered on money, utility-bill protections, local jobs, and transparency.

In October, Amazon announced “Built Together,” pledging more than $1 billion over five years to U.S. communities hosting its data centers. Amazon also pledged to publish its annual energy and water use, install lower-emission backup generators at new sites, and pay enough for power to avoid increasing other customers’ electricity bills.

In January, Microsoft promised to cover the power infrastructure costs associated with its facilities and stop seeking local property-tax breaks. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google also dropped requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements regarding data center projects.

That may not be enough in states like Texas. Incoming Gov. Hinojosa has called for repealing data center tax breaks and requiring developers to protect household utility bills and local water supplies, while giving residents more say over new projects.

“The impact may ultimately be less about restrictions than extracting more from data center operators for the social license to operate through taxes, power rates, environmental considerations, and community support,” analysts at investment banking firm Macquarie Group Limited wrote in a note Wednesday.

AI cloud providers could face higher rents for power-equipped data center buildings needed to fulfill customer contracts, potentially passing those costs on to customers, the analysts wrote. Demand from large cloud companies and AI labs could further tighten the supply of available sites. Big Tech companies may also fall back on upgrading or retrofitting existing data centers, Dell’Oro’s Fung said.

Many analysts and tech industry experts agree on one thing: Even with restrictions, AI centers are here to stay, especially as hyperscalers say they need more computing capacity online, not less. Amazon, Microsoft, Google parent Alphabet, and Meta are projected to spend between $720 billion and $740 billion in combined capital expenditures for calendar 2026.

In a call with analysts on Oct. 28, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said accelerating demand led the company to add 24 new data centers across five continents during the past quarter. A day later, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects revenue growth in the company’s cloud business to be 40% or more in 2027 and 2028, largely from AI.

“We’re installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up,” he said.

#5422. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5421. Your First Instinct in a Crisis Is Probably Wrong. Here’s What Strong Leaders Do.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

What do you do when your first reaction goes sideways?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

You probably believe you will be the calm one when something goes wrong. You picture yourself absorbing the bad news, asking the right questions and setting a steady course while everyone around you scrambles. Then the phone rings late on a Friday, and the first thing that happens is not a thought. It is a reaction.

That reaction feels like clarity. It shows up instantly, it carries total confidence and it arrives with a jolt of urgency that makes waiting feel irresponsible. The trouble is, it often solves a different problem than the one in front of you. Learning to notice that gap, and to cross it on purpose, is one of the most useful skills you can build as a leader.

Under acute stress, your body does what it was built to do. Your heart rate climbs, your attention narrows and your brain favors speed over nuance. That response works well when a threat is physical and immediate. It works poorly when the threat is ambiguous, involves many people and will unfold over days or weeks.

Narrow focus helps when danger is right in front of you. It becomes a liability when the information you need is scattered across a team, a customer inbox and a conversation that has not happened yet. In that moment, the urge to act right now can feel like leadership. More often, it is discomfort looking for an exit. Panic rarely leads to sound choices, which is why staying calm lets you lead a team through a crisis rather than react.

Most crisis missteps fall into a few familiar patterns.

The first is the urge to fix it immediately. Speed feels responsible, but acting before you understand the scope often creates a second problem on top of the first.

The second is the urge to explain everything. When you feel exposed, you want to fill the silence with context and justification. Long explanations offered early tend to sound defensive, and they lock you into details that may change as more facts surface.

The third is the urge to find out who is at fault. Assigning blame can feel like taking control, yet it shifts your team’s energy from solving the problem to protecting themselves.

The fourth is the urge to go quiet. Silence can feel safe, but the people who depend on you will fill an information vacuum with their own assumptions and those assumptions are rarely generous.

The goal is not to ignore your first instinct. It is to give it a brief review before it becomes a decision. In most situations, even serious ones, you have more time than the adrenaline suggests. Ninety seconds is almost always available.

Use that window to ask three questions. What do I actually know, versus what I fear? Who is affected, including people who have not said anything yet? What happens if I wait one hour before responding publicly?

It also helps to look at the problem the way an outsider would. Stepping outside your role for a moment creates enough distance to separate facts from feelings. Write down what you know on one side of a page and what you assume on the other. The second column is usually longer than you expect.

None of this means waiting for perfect information. You will rarely have it, and acting decisively, then adjusting as you learn, usually beats freezing. The point is to make your first move considered rather than reflexive.

The second instinct, the one that arrives after the initial surge passes, is usually better calibrated. It considers the timeline. It accounts for the audience. It notices what you can control and what you cannot.

You can strengthen that second instinct long before any crisis arrives. Decide in advance who has the authority to speak, who needs to be in the first conversation and where the reliable facts will live. Talk through a few plausible scenarios with your team while everyone is calm. When the real moment comes, you’ll choose from options you have already considered instead of inventing them under pressure.

It also helps to spread the thinking around. Leaders who listen actively and push decisions closer to the people with firsthand information tend to see problems more completely. The person closest to the issue often knows something you don’t, and a crisis is the worst time to discover you never asked.

Teams that handle difficult moments well rarely have to improvise. They simply have to improvise less.

When things settle, people rarely recall the exact words you used. They remember whether your response felt proportionate, whether you addressed their real concern and whether your account held up as new information emerged. Employees, customers and partners who never said a word watch for the same thing: evidence that you handled the situation with care and judgment.

That impression forms quickly, often within the first day, and it is built from small choices. Your first instinct will rarely get it all right. A short, deliberate pause gives you a much better chance.

You probably believe you will be the calm one when something goes wrong. You picture yourself absorbing the bad news, asking the right questions and setting a steady course while everyone around you scrambles. Then the phone rings late on a Friday, and the first thing that happens is not a thought. It is a reaction.

That reaction feels like clarity. It shows up instantly, it carries total confidence and it arrives with a jolt of urgency that makes waiting feel irresponsible. The trouble is, it often solves a different problem than the one in front of you. Learning to notice that gap, and to cross it on purpose, is one of the most useful skills you can build as a leader.

Under acute stress, your body does what it was built to do. Your heart rate climbs, your attention narrows and your brain favors speed over nuance. That response works well when a threat is physical and immediate. It works poorly when the threat is ambiguous, involves many people and will unfold over days or weeks.

#5420. ‘Seismic’ blue wave triggers the sinking of oil prices, energy stocks, and the chances of power permitting reform

Most energy stocks plunged on Wednesday—except for clean power and utilities in a few remaining reliably red states—as crude oil prices fell to one-month lows because of bullishness on Iran war peace talks and bearishness on the data center boom after Democratic blue wave wins in the midterm elections.

Even as Wall Street celebrated the anticipated gridlock from a splintered Congress and White House—the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 3% Wednesday—most energy companies moved in the opposite direction, especially in states such as Texas that had the most shocking Democratic wins.

The other potential loser is the bipartisan legislation to expedite the construction of energy projects—and power the AI boom—that would benefit both renewable power and oil and gas pipelines. Anti-fossil fuel Democrats are now potentially motivated to take harder negotiating tactics. TD Cowen analysts slashed their projection for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) from 40% to 25% during the lame-duck session before the new Congress is sworn in.

Charles Hua, executive director of the PowerLines nonprofit, said the “seismic” blue wave from Congress to governors’ elections to public service commissions was a referendum on spiking utility bills, gasoline costs, and the inflationary ripple effects throughout the economy.

“You only get such seismicity in political results if something is fundamentally unsteady or unstable, and I think one of the big manifestations of that really has been energy costs,” Hua told Fortune.

In addition to voter discontent over the Iran war and fuel prices, there were more than 40 local ballot measure on restricting or regulating data centers. All but one of them—in North Dakota—passed. “That’s a staggering statistic,” Hua said.

As for Wall Street performance, there were clear winners and losers by utilities and independent power producers.

NRG Energy and Vistra, which are building out gas-fired power generation in Texas to help fuel the AI boom, saw their stock values drop precipitously by 12% and 15%, respectively. Gas turbine manufacturer GE Vernova dipped by 10%.

Analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies specifically highlighted the “Texas shock,” noting that “the most impactful surprise is the magnitude by which Texas voted Democratic, imperiling the outlook for data center developments.”

Texas-based Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk—after unsuccessfully spending hundreds of millions on GOP candidates—posted on X, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

On the other hand, utilities that operate in Florida, which remained Republican, were rewarded. Florida-based NextEra Energy jumped 5% and Duke Energy rose by 3%.

With more clean energy-loving Democrats coming into power, renewable energy companies also were rewarded. First Solar rose by over 4% and solar parts manufacturer Nextpower spiked by 13%.

After President Donald Trump downplayed the potential for an escalation in Iran and Vice President JD Vance blamed his party’s election losses on the war, the global oil benchmark fell by 8% to below $100 per barrel for the first time in nearly a month. As such, oil producers and refiners suffered on Wall Street too.

ExxonMobil and Chevron dipped by 4% and 5%, respectively. Refiners Marathon Petroleum and Valero Energy, which have reported record profits of late, plunged by 9% and 7%, respectively.

“We had a referendum on inflation, high oil prices, and Trump in general,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm. “It feels like Trump will have more pushback and less maneuverability around how he wants to conduct the conflict in Iran.”

There may be optimism for peace talks in Iran, but this war likely is far from over, Pickering warned.

There is no clear compromise yet, and Trump could easily get frustrated and opt for escalation between now and January, which is what Trump himself predicted before the election.

“I think the Iran conflict gets more complicated for the U.S. We’ve been looking for an off ramp, but we want an off ramp that doesn’t leave the Middle East in chaos,” Pickering told Fortune. “I think that issue probably transcends the election. Even with more Democrats, I don’t think they’re going to want a bad outcome for the Iran crisis. Oil is down, but it’s not cratering.”

Domestically, much of the focus will remain on the data center backlash and permitting reform. Some of the biggest states for data center growth are Texas, Georgia, and Ohio and Democratic challengers all won the governor elections in those states while pushing for data center moratoriums.

“‘Moratorium’ certainly is the buzzword,” Hua said, but it’s not clear if those efforts equate to temporary pauses or outright opposition. “How high on the priory list is electricity? I suspect that electricity vis-a-vis data centers will remain a top-of-mind issue for these new administrations.”

The AI boom has brought both parties somewhat closer together in terms of supporting all-of-the-above energy solutions. That’s why a bipartisan permitting reform effort focused on expediting energy construction of all kinds was coming together. But a Democratic wave is expected to leave more of them arguing in favor of waiting until next year to propose a version that’s less friendly to fossil fuel projects. Such an effort could be risky because it would still require Trump’s signature.

“With greater leverage heading into 2027, Democrats have less incentive to accept pipeline provisions during the lame duck, pushing the debate toward a narrower clean energy-transmission package or no deal,” Dumoulin-Smith added.

The legislation would facilitate the growth of long-distance transmission lines, which most benefit renewable energy. As such, top transmission developer Quanta Services saw its stock fall by 12% Wednesday.

The legislation’s Democratic sponsor, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., implored his party to still support the bill on Wednesday.

“Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises,” Whitehouse told Fortune in a statement. “It’s a bird in the hand. We’d be fools not to take it.”

Jordan Blum is the Energy editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of a growing global energy sector for oil and gas, transition businesses, renewables, and critical minerals.

#5419. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5418. The Hidden Risks of Building Your Own Delivery Fleet as a Growing Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Building an in-house delivery fleet may seem like a smart way to reduce costs and gain greater control, but these challenges can quickly impact profitability.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The invoices from the regional carrier keep getting bigger. For the owner of a growing home furnishings retailer, delivery has become one of the largest expenses outside of inventory, and the complaints that come with it — missed windows, damaged pieces, vague updates — still land on her desk.

So she runs the numbers on three cargo vans and three full-time drivers. On paper, the savings look obvious. What the spreadsheet leaves out is that she is not just buying vans. She is starting a transportation operation inside a company built to sell furniture.

The case for in-house delivery is legitimate. You decide when orders go out and how customers are treated at the door. You depend less on a third party’s capacity during busy weeks, you can coordinate dispatch directly with inventory, and at sufficient volume, you may lower your cost per delivery.

The catch is that an outside carrier bundles its costs into a price per stop. Once you own the operation, those costs scatter. Maintenance appears in repair invoices, insurance in renewal paperwork, depreciation on the balance sheet and recruiting and supervision both in payroll and in the owner’s calendar. Vehicles also sit idle on slow days and break down on busy ones.

In-house delivery is not automatically cheaper. Build a fully loaded cost per delivery that includes idle time, downtime, fuel, insurance, depreciation and management hours, then compare it with outsourced pricing across slow weeks as well as peak ones. A model built on your best month will flatter the fleet.

The same principle applies to broader ecommerce operations. Growing order volumes require companies to reconsider operational processes, technology investments and cost structures.

With two vans, the owner knows who drove which route and when the oil was last changed. That informality works, which is why it tends to persist long after it should be replaced.

At 10, 20 or 50 vehicles, decisions that once lived in one person’s head need to live in a system. Assign ownership for scheduling, maintenance, driver qualification files and performance. In a smaller operation, that may be one capable operations manager, but it must be a named role. Then track a short list of numbers: on-time rate, cost per delivery, vehicle downtime and incidents. Without them, you are managing by anecdote.

This transition reflects a broader challenge of business expansion. Building systems and teams that scale successfully emphasizes the importance of repeatable processes, clear responsibilities and infrastructure that can support increasing operational demands.

A driver is often the only person from your company a customer meets, and also the person operating a heavy vehicle on public roads with your inventory inside. Informal hiring does not scale. A repeatable process does.

Define written qualification criteria, including license status, driving history review where permitted and experience suited to your vehicles, and apply them to every candidate. Onboarding should cover cargo height and clearance, securing loads, customer handoffs and what to do when something goes wrong.

Put your standards for company vehicle use in writing, including phone use, personal use and defect reporting. Some vehicle sizes and operations trigger additional federal or local requirements, so verify what applies to your fleet.

Imagine a company that advertises tight two-hour windows and stacks routes to hit them. It works until a customer isn’t home or a freeway slows. Now the driver is behind, and the easiest way to recover is to speed up, skip a break or glance at a phone.

Fleet safety is partly a scheduling problem. If your routes only work when nothing goes wrong, you have designed in pressure. A few practical fixes help:

Tight windows can remain a selling point where routes are dense and predictable.

Reliable delivery also depends on operational consistency. Efficient workflows and well-organized teams help businesses maintain service standards as demand increases.

Relying on drivers to notice mechanical problems works for a few vehicles. It fails once drivers rotate through different vans and each assumes someone else reported the strange noise.

Set preventive service intervals based on manufacturer guidance and actual use. Require a short pre-trip inspection and make defect reporting penalty-free. Keep records in one place so patterns become visible, such as a van that keeps returning to the shop. Decide in advance that a vehicle with a safety-related problem comes out of service, even on a heavy day.

Then plan for downtime. A spare vehicle, a rental arrangement or an outside carrier on standby keeps one broken van from becoming a week of broken promises. Customers experience your maintenance program as reliability.

Most owners picture an accident as a repair bill. The real cost is wider: employee injuries, injuries to other road users, vehicle replacement, insurance claims and possible premium changes, delayed orders, lost productivity, administrative work and reputational damage. Depending on the circumstances, it can also raise legal questions, which is one reason consistent records matter.

The human side deserves honest attention. Delivery vans and box trucks are often heavier and taller than the passenger cars around them, and the injuries associated with commercial vehicle collisions, including head trauma, spinal damage and fractures, can change someone’s life and disrupt a business for a long time.

A one-page accident procedure, reviewed with every driver, should answer a few questions:

A business that outsources delivery pushes much of its transportation risk onto the carrier. Once you operate your own vehicles, that risk is yours to evaluate.

Work with a qualified broker to review limits, exclusions, covered drivers and how cargo is treated. Pay particular attention to the difference between company-owned vehicles and employees’ personal vehicles used for business, since those situations are often treated differently. Requirements and policy terms vary by jurisdiction and insurer, so confirm the details for your own operation.

Insurance also cannot replace good systems. Coverage helps absorb a loss. It does nothing to prevent the missed inspection, the rushed route or the untrained hire.

Sustainable growth requires systems that can operate consistently without constant intervention from the business owner. This principle is explored in an Entrepreneur article about building repeatable systems for long-term business growth, highlighting the importance of documenting, evaluating and continuously improving business processes.

Owning vehicles buys control, but control only pays off through discipline: clear ownership, consistent hiring, realistic schedules, preventive maintenance, an accident plan and a sober view of cost. The businesses that succeed with in-house delivery do so because they built a system around their vans, not because they bought good ones.

The invoices from the regional carrier keep getting bigger. For the owner of a growing home furnishings retailer, delivery has become one of the largest expenses outside of inventory, and the complaints that come with it — missed windows, damaged pieces, vague updates — still land on her desk.

So she runs the numbers on three cargo vans and three full-time drivers. On paper, the savings look obvious. What the spreadsheet leaves out is that she is not just buying vans. She is starting a transportation operation inside a company built to sell furniture.

The case for in-house delivery is legitimate. You decide when orders go out and how customers are treated at the door. You depend less on a third party’s capacity during busy weeks, you can coordinate dispatch directly with inventory, and at sufficient volume, you may lower your cost per delivery.

#5417. Appeals court tosses lawsuit over Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax rollout, ruling homeowners can’t sue over notices

A New York appeals court on Wednesday threw out a lawsuit over the rollout of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax, ruling that the homeowners who sued had not adequately shown they were harmed.

The Appellate Division, Second Department, reversed a Sept. 29 judgment by Staten Island Supreme Court Justice Wayne Ozzi that had granted the homeowners injunctive and declaratory relief. The four-judge panel was unanimous. It denied the petition and dismissed the case a week after hearing arguments.

Seven homeowners, represented by former First Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro, sued the city in August. They challenged the Department of Finance’s publication of a supplemental roll of about 900,000 properties and the roughly 17,000 notices it mailed to owners who might owe the surcharge, arguing the city made owners prove they live in their homes instead of checking its own records first.

The court did not rule on that argument. It found the homeowners lacked standing, or the legal right to sue, because they showed no concrete injury. Appearing on the roll or receiving a notice wasn’t enough, the judges wrote. The notice, court documents read, “serves an informational purpose,” like a debt collection letter, and the state legislature “must have anticipated that the list of notice recipients would not be exact or flawless,” or it would not have created an exemption process.

The court also said the rollout confusion was too “generalized, tenuous, and ephemeral” to count as an injury. It said the homeowners offered no evidence that anyone had misused the information or that they faced stalking or fraud, and it noted that the city’s annual assessment rolls already list each owner’s name, assessed value and market value. The court also said that the cost of applying for an exemption was not enough cause for injury, as all taxpayers spend time and money complying with tax rules, and the homeowners had not documented or quantified their costs.

Two of the seven petitioners, Rachel O’Brien and Carmine Morano, never alleged they received a notice. The other five were exempted after the suit was filed.

The panel sided with the homeowners on two points: It rejected the city’s argument that exempting the petitioners made the case moot, and its argument that the tax law limits challenges to appeals before the city’s Tax Commission. It also declined to decide whether DOF broke its own rule by not relying on 2024 income-tax data when it chose who got notices.

The ruling does not settle the tax’s other legal fights. Gothamist reported the surcharge faces three separate challenges.

The city has also changed course since the notices went out. After the state sent early 2025 income-tax data on Aug. 12, DOF cleared 1,210 owners and said it would send new letters to about 10,800 others. Gothamist reported that DOF has now granted more than 8,800 exemption requests. Comptroller Mark Levine estimated earlier this year the tax could raise up to $380 million from about 11,200 properties. Mamdani has said it will raise $500 million a year.

In a statement, Mamdani said the court “rejected an attempt by the ultrawealthy to avoid paying their fair share.” He added: “But owning a second home worth over $5 million should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable.”

He said the city will keep defending the law against “ongoing challenges in Suffolk County,” brought by “some of the same uberwealthy interests whose arguments just lost in court today.”

He closed: “We will implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone.”

#5416. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.
